q023.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains an Apache Spark job definition named Job1.

You have an Azure SQL database named Source1 that has public internet access disabled.

You need to ensure that Job1 can access the data in Source1.

What should you create?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: a managed private endpoint

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Why "a managed private endpoint" is correct: In the Microsoft Fabric network architecture, when you need data engineering workloads (such as notebooks or Apache Spark jobs) to access Azure platform as a service (PaaS) data sources, such as an Azure SQL database, that have public internet access disabled, you must use a managed private endpoint. When you provision this endpoint within a Fabric workspace (which must have a managed virtual network enabled), a secure, private connection is created through Azure Private Link directly to the Azure SQL database, bypassing the public internet restriction.

  • Official documentation: Managed private endpoints in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Why the other options are incorrect:

A. an on-premises data gateway: This gateway is designed to connect cloud services to data sources hosted on on-premises networks or on virtual machines (IaaS), not to connect natively to Azure PaaS services such as Azure SQL Database, which integrate far more efficiently and securely through Azure Private Link.

  • Official documentation: What is an on-premises data gateway? - Microsoft Fabric

C. an integration runtime: This is a compute infrastructure concept used natively in Azure Data Factory (ADF) and Azure Synapse Analytics for data pipelines. In Microsoft Fabric, Apache Spark workloads use the built-in Spark pools and the workspace's managed virtual network (managed VNet) for private routing, not a separate integration runtime.

  • Official documentation: Fabric networking concepts compared with Azure (Integration Runtime) - Microsoft Fabric

D. a data management gateway: "Data Management Gateway" is a legacy, obsolete technology term that Microsoft formerly used to refer to what is now the on-premises data gateway. It is incorrect for the same reason as option A, in addition to using discontinued terminology.

  • Official documentation: On-premises data gateway release history and versions - Microsoft Learn

q024.stem:
You have an Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 account named storage1 and an Amazon S3 bucket named storage2.

You have the Delta Parquet files shown in the following table.

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that has the cache for shortcuts enabled. Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 has the following shortcuts:

A shortcut to ProductFile aliased as Products

A shortcut to StoreFile aliased as Stores

A shortcut to TripsFile aliased as Trips

The data from which shortcuts will be retrieved from the cache?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Stores only

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Why "Stores only" is correct: The OneLake shortcut caching feature is designed specifically to optimize performance and reduce data egress costs when reading files from external clouds. For a file to enter the cache, it must meet two inflexible rules:

  1. Supported source: The cache currently supports only shortcuts that point to Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage (GCS).

  2. Size limit: Only files smaller than 1 GB are cached.

The StoreFile (Stores) file meets both conditions perfectly: it is stored in an Amazon S3 bucket (storage2) and its size is 25 MB. Therefore, it is the only shortcut that will use the cache.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcut caching (Supported sources and limitations) - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Trips and Stores only, and E. Products, Stores, and Trips: Both options include the "Trips" shortcut (TripsFile). Although this file is in a supported external source (Amazon S3), its size is 2 GB. Because it exceeds the maximum limit of 1 GB per file, the Fabric engine excludes TripsFile from the cache and reads its data by querying the original bucket directly every time.

  • Official documentation: OneLake caching size limitations - Microsoft Fabric

B. Products and Store only, and D. Products only: These options wrongly include the Products shortcut (ProductFile). Although its size of 50 MB is below the limit, this file is stored in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (ADLS Gen2) (storage1). In Fabric, reading from ADLS Gen2 already happens within the Azure backbone bandwidth, so shortcut caching is neither supported nor applied for these native sources.

  • Official documentation: Cached data source limitations (ADLS Gen2 exclusion) - Microsoft Fabric

q025.stem:
HOTSPOT -

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains the items shown in the following table.

For Model1, the Keep your Direct Lake data up to date option is disabled.

You need to configure the execution of the items to meet the following requirements:

Notebook1 must execute every weekday at 8:00 AM.

Notebook2 must execute when a file is saved to an Azure Blob Storage container.

Model1 must refresh when Notebook1 has executed successfully.

How should you orchestrate each item? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Notebook1: Add Notebook1 to Pipeline1.

  • Notebook2: From Real-Time hub, configure the execution of Notebook2.

  • Pipeline1: Configure the execution of Pipeline1 by using a schedule.

  • Model1: Add Model1 to Pipeline1.

Detailed analysis for Notebook1

Why "Add Notebook1 to Pipeline1." is correct: The requirement states that Notebook1 and Model1 must be chained (the model must be refreshed after the notebook succeeds). Data pipelines in Fabric are designed specifically for orchestration and for creating sequential logical dependencies. By adding Notebook1 to a pipeline, you can link its output ("On success") to the next activity.

  • Official documentation: Notebook activity in Azure Data Factory and Synapse pipelines - Microsoft Fabric

Why the other options are incorrect for Notebook1:

Add Notebook1 to an Apache Spark job definition: A Spark job definition runs the notebook in isolation as a batch, but it does not offer native graphical tools to chain automatic dependencies with semantic models after it completes.

  • Official documentation: What is an Apache Spark job definition? - Microsoft Fabric

From Real-Time hub, configure the execution of Notebook1: Real-Time hub is designed to react to streaming events or state changes, not to orchestrate sequential batch workflows (such as chaining notebooks with models).

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric Real-Time hub - Microsoft Fabric

Detailed analysis for Notebook2

Why "From Real-Time hub, configure the execution of Notebook2." is correct: The case requires this notebook to run driven by an external event ("when a file is saved to an Azure Blob Storage container"). In Fabric, Real-Time hub integrates with Azure Event Grid to detect external events (such as the creation of a blob in Azure Storage) and can react to them by triggering actions through Data Activator, such as running a Fabric item.

  • Official documentation: Get Azure Blob Storage events in Real-Time hub - Microsoft Fabric

Why the other options are incorrect for Notebook2:

Add Notebook2 to an Apache Spark job definition: A job definition does not have native triggers based on external events coming from Azure storage.

  • Official documentation: Schedule and run Spark job definitions - Microsoft Fabric

Add Notebook2 to Pipeline1: Pipeline1 is going to be configured to run on a strict schedule (8:00 AM) to meet the first requirement, so it cannot be used at the same time to react asynchronously to file creation events.

  • Official documentation: Triggers in data pipelines - Microsoft Fabric

Detailed analysis for Pipeline1

Why "Configure the execution of Pipeline1 by using a schedule." is correct: The requirement demands that Notebook1 (now inside Pipeline1) run "every weekday at 8:00 AM". Data pipelines in Fabric include scheduled triggers that let you precisely define recurring schedules (days, hours, minutes).

  • Official documentation: Schedule a data pipeline run - Microsoft Fabric

Why the other options are incorrect for Pipeline1:

Add Pipeline1 to an Apache Spark job definition: It is hierarchically impossible and incorrect to add an orchestration pipeline inside a Spark job definition.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to Spark and pipeline integration - Microsoft Fabric

From Real-Time hub, configure the execution of Pipeline1: Real-Time hub responds to events and continuous data streams. For strictly time-based execution, the pipeline's built-in scheduler is the correct, native tool.

  • Official documentation: Real-Time hub vs Data Factory - Microsoft Fabric

Detailed analysis for Model1

Why "Add Model1 to Pipeline1." is correct: The requirement states that the model must be refreshed only after Notebook1 runs successfully. Since we have orchestrated the notebook in Pipeline1, adding the Semantic model refresh activity to this same pipeline and connecting it through a success path ("On success") from the Notebook1 activity mathematically guarantees that this logical dependency is met.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model refresh activity in Data Factory - Microsoft Fabric

Why the other options are incorrect for Model1:

Set Keep your Direct Lake data up to date to On: The question statement explicitly invalidates this option by indicating: "For Model1, the option to keep your Direct Lake data up to date is turned off" (and it may be off for business reasons, to avoid inconsistent reads). In addition, this option is an autonomous detection mechanism; it does not respect the strict requirement to refresh only when the notebook finishes.

  • Official documentation: Manage Direct Lake semantic models (Automatic updates) - Microsoft Fabric

From Real-Time hub, configure Model1 to refresh: The semantic model refresh must be the consequent step in a batch flow that depends on the notebook. Real-Time hub is not designed to orchestrate this dependent chaining.

  • Official documentation: Orchestrating semantic model refreshes - Microsoft Fabric

q026.stem:
Your company has a sales department that uses two Fabric workspaces named Workspace1 and Workspace2.

The company decides to implement a domain strategy to organize the workspaces.

You need to ensure that a user can perform the following tasks:

Create a new domain for the sales department.

Create two subdomains: one for the east region and one for the west region.

Assign Workspace1 to the east region subdomain.

Assign Workspace2 to the west region subdomain.

The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.

Which role should you assign to the user?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Fabric admin

Detailed analysis for the correct option

Why "Fabric admin" is correct: The scenario requires the user to perform a sequence of tasks, and the first of them is "Create a new domain for the sales department". In the Microsoft Fabric architecture, creating a root domain is a tenant-level setting. Only Fabric admins (as well as global administrators or Power BI administrators) have the permissions needed to create new domains. Although lower roles can perform the remaining tasks (creating subdomains and assigning workspaces), the creation of the top-level domain makes the Fabric admin role the least-privileged role that can complete the full list of requirements.

  • Official documentation: Create a domain in Microsoft Fabric (Prerequisites) - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Why the other options are incorrect:

A. workspace Admin: Workspace admins have control only within the boundaries of their workspace. They do not have tenant-level privileges to create corporate domains or organizational subdomains. They could only associate their workspace with a domain if the global setting allows it.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Fabric

B. domain admin: Domain admins can fully manage a domain once it has been created. They have permissions to create the subdomains (East and West) and assign the workspaces, but the Fabric engine prevents them from creating a root domain from scratch, because that action requires tenant-level administration privileges.

  • Official documentation: Domain roles (Domain admin) - Microsoft Fabric

C. domain contributor: The domain contributor role is a very low-privilege role designed exclusively to let certain users assign workspaces to an existing domain or subdomain. A contributor cannot create domains or subdomains, so it fails three of the four requirements in the scenario.

  • Official documentation: Domain roles (Domain contributor) - Microsoft Fabric

q027.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a warehouse named DW1 and a data pipeline named Pipeline1.

You plan to add a user named User3 to Workspace1.

You need to ensure that User3 can perform the following actions:

View all the items in Workspace1.

Update the tables in DW1.

The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.

You already assigned the appropriate object-level permissions to DW1.

Which workspace role should you assign to User3?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Viewer

Detailed analysis for the correct option

Why "Viewer" is correct: The principle of least privilege requires granting only the level of access strictly necessary to perform a task. The workspace-level Viewer role meets the first requirement by allowing User3 to "view all items in Workspace1" and to connect to the SQL endpoint. The deciding factor in this question is the statement: "You have already assigned the appropriate object-level permissions to DW1". In the Fabric security architecture, the best practice for granting granular write permissions (such as updating specific tables) without compromising the rest of the environment is to assign the Viewer role in the workspace and grant object-level SQL permissions (e.g., GRANT UPDATE). If a higher role were assigned, the user would have modify privileges over Pipeline1 or other items, violating the security principle.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces (Combining the Viewer role with granular permissions) - Microsoft Fabric and Granular security in the data warehouse - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Admin: The Admin role has full and absolute control over the workspace, including the ability to add/remove users, modify security and delete critical items. This drastically violates the principle of least privilege.

  • Official documentation: Admin role permissions in workspaces - Microsoft Fabric

B. Member: The Member role allows modifying and deleting all the items in the workspace (including Pipeline1), as well as sharing items and publishing apps. It far exceeds the privileges needed.

  • Official documentation: Member role permissions in workspaces - Microsoft Fabric

D. Contributor: The Contributor role grants global create, edit and delete permissions over all the items in the workspace. Assigning this role would make the previous configuration of "object-level permissions" useless, because the user would automatically inherit full write access (Read/Write) over the entire warehouse and over the data pipeline, breaking the principle of least privilege.

  • Official documentation: Contributor role permissions in workspaces - Microsoft Fabric

q028.stem:
You have a Fabric capacity that contains a workspace named Workspace1.

Workspace1 contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1, a data pipeline, a notebook, and several Microsoft Power BI reports.

A user named User1 wants to use SQL to analyze the data in Lakehouse1.

You need to configure access for User1. The solution must meet the following requirements:

Provide User1 with read access to the table data in Lakehouse1.

Prevent User1 from using Apache Spark to query the underlying files in Lakehouse1.

Prevent User1 from accessing other items in Workspace1.

What should you do?
options: Share Lakehouse1 with User1 directly and select Read all SQL endpoint data.
Assign User1 the Viewer role for Workspace1. Share Lakehouse1 with User1 and select Read all SQL endpoint data.
Share Lakehouse1 with User1 directly and select Build reports on the default semantic model.
Assign User1 the Member role for Workspace1. Share Lakehouse1 with User1 and select Read all SQL endpoint data.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Share Lakehouse1 with User1 directly and select Read all SQL endpoint data.

Detailed analysis for the correct option

Why "Share Lakehouse1 with User1 directly and select Read all SQL endpoint data" is correct: To meet the strict limitation that the user cannot access any other item in the workspace (such as the pipeline, the notebook or the reports), you must use item-level sharing. Sharing the lakehouse directly without giving access to the workspace fully isolates this user from the rest of the items. In addition, by specifically selecting the "Read all SQL endpoint data" option (ReadData), the user is granted the exact permission to connect to the SQL analytics endpoint and run T-SQL queries against the tables. By not selecting "Read all Apache Spark" (ReadAll), the user is explicitly denied access to the underlying OneLake files through notebooks or Spark jobs, meeting all three requirements perfectly.

  • Official documentation: Share a lakehouse and manage permissions - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Assign User1 the Viewer role for Workspace1. Share Lakehouse1...: Assigning the Viewer role at the Fabric workspace level gives the user the right to see the existence of all the items contained in that workspace (the notebook, the pipeline, the reports). This directly violates the third requirement ("Prevent User1 from accessing other items in Workspace1").

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces (Viewer role permissions) - Microsoft Fabric

C. Share Lakehouse1 with User1 directly and select Build reports on the default semantic model: The build reports option grants the Build permission on the underlying semantic model. This permission is designed to let users create and publish reports in Power BI by using the lakehouse data, but it does not grant direct database-level access to run custom SQL queries through the SQL endpoint.

  • Official documentation: Semantic model sharing and Build permissions - Microsoft Fabric

D. Assign User1 the Member role for Workspace1. Share Lakehouse1...: The Member role is a high-privilege role that allows modifying, deleting and managing permissions on all the items in the workspace. This not only violates the restriction on accessing other items, but also completely destroys the principle of least privilege and would give implicit Spark access to the physical files.

  • Official documentation: Roles in workspaces (Member role permissions) - Microsoft Fabric

Roles in workspaces (Viewer role permissions) - Microsoft Fabric
Semantic model sharing and Build permissions - Microsoft Fabric

q029.stem:
DRAG DROP -

You are implementing the following data entities in a Fabric environment:

Entity1: Available in a lakehouse and contains data that will be used as a core organization entity

Entity2: Available in a semantic model and contains data that meets organizational standards

Entity3: Available in a Microsoft Power BI report and contains data that is ready for sharing and reuse

Entity4: Available in a Power BI dashboard and contains approved data for executive-level decision making

Your company requires that specific governance processes be implemented for the data.

You need to apply endorsement badges to the entities based on each entity’s use case.

Which badge should you apply to each entity? To answer, drag the appropriate badges the correct entities. Each badge may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Entity1: Master data

  • Entity2: Certified

  • Entity3: Promoted

  • Entity4: Cannot be endorsed

Detailed analysis for each entity

Why "Master data" is correct for Entity1: Entity1 resides in a lakehouse and is described as the "central entity of the organization". In the Microsoft Fabric governance framework, the "Master data" badge is designed exclusively for items that the organization considers its core or its single source of truth, such as customer catalogs or product master data. In addition, this is the only endorsement badge that strictly requires the item to contain underlying physical data, which applies perfectly to a lakehouse or warehouse.

  • Official documentation: Endorsement overview - Master data - Microsoft Fabric

Why "Certified" is correct for Entity2: Entity2 is a semantic model that is explicitly specified as containing data that "meets organizational standards". The "Certified" badge is used for exactly this scenario: it indicates that the item has been reviewed by authorized reviewers and has passed the company's quality controls and standards, which makes it an official, reliable and safe source for critical decision-making across the organization.

  • Official documentation: Endorsement overview - Certification - Microsoft Fabric

Why "Promoted" is correct for Entity3: Entity3 is a Power BI report described as "ready to share and reuse". The "Promoted" badge is designed for agile collaborative work. It allows content creators and owners themselves (without requiring the intervention of a Fabric admin) to highlight reports or semantic models that they have validated in their department and that they consider valuable enough to be shared and reused by other users.

  • Official documentation: Endorsement overview - Promotion - Microsoft Fabric

Why "Cannot be endorsed" is correct for Entity4: Entity4 is a Power BI dashboard. Although the description is tempting in mentioning "data approved for executive-level decision-making", reality is governed by a fixed technical limitation of the platform architecture. Currently, dashboards are the only Power BI item that does not support any type of endorsement badge. You can certify or promote the semantic model or the report they are based on, but the dashboard itself "cannot be endorsed".

  • Official documentation: Limitations of items supported for endorsement (Dashboard exclusion) - Microsoft Fabric

q030.stem:
HOTSPOT -

You have three users named User1, User2, and User3.

You have the Fabric workspaces shown in the following table.

You have a security group named Group1 that contains User1 and User3.

The Fabric admin creates the domains shown in the following table.

User1 creates a new workspace named Workspace3.

You add Group1 to the default domain of Domain1.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • User3 has Viewer role access to Workspace3: No

  • User3 has Domain contributor access to Domain1: Yes

  • User2 has Contributor role access to Workspace3: No

Detailed analysis for each statement

Why "No" is correct for the first statement (User3 has Viewer role access to Workspace3): In the Microsoft Fabric architecture, domains are logical boundaries for data governance and organization, but they are not access security boundaries. Belonging to a security group (Group1) linked to a domain does not magically grant any read or write permission (such as Viewer or Contributor) over individual workspaces. Since User1 independently created "Workspace3", User1 is the only initial admin. User3 will not have access to Workspace3 unless permissions are explicitly shared at the workspace level.

  • Official documentation: Access control in workspaces vs. domains - Microsoft Fabric

Why "Yes" is correct for the second statement (User3 has Domain contributor access to Domain1): When an admin configures the Default domain option and adds a security group (in this case, Group1) to that list, the Fabric engine automatically associates any new workspace created by those users with that domain. So that the system can perform this assignment in the background, the interface implicitly and automatically grants the Domain contributor role to the members of that group. Therefore, since User3 is a member of Group1, User3 does receive this level of access over Domain1 natively.

  • Official documentation: Configure a default domain (Automatic Contributor assignment) - Microsoft Fabric

Why "No" is correct for the third statement (User2 has Contributor role access to Workspace3): User2 is the admin of Workspace2 and Domain2. There is no cross-security relationship, group membership or permission inheritance between User2 and the new workspace created by User1 (Workspace3). Therefore, User2 lacks any level of access (including Contributor) to Workspace3.

  • Official documentation: Roles and permissions in Microsoft Fabric workspaces - Microsoft Fabric

links.t: Access control in workspaces vs. domains - Microsoft Fabric
Configure a default domain (Automatic Contributor assignment) - Microsoft Fabric

q031.stem:
You have two Fabric workspaces named Workspace1 and Workspace2.

You have a Fabric deployment pipeline named deployPipeline1 that deploys items from Workspace1 to Workspace2. DeployPipeline1 contains all the items in Workspace1.

You recently modified the items in Workspaces1.

The workspaces currently contain the items shown in the following table.

Items in Workspace1 that have the same name as items in Workspace2 are currently paired.

You need to ensure that the items in Workspace1 overwrite the corresponding items in Workspace2. The solution must minimize effort.

What should you do?
options: Delete all the items in Workspace2, and then run deployPipeline1.
Rename each item in Workspace2 to have the same name as the items in Workspace1.
Back up the items in Workspace2, and then run deployPipeline1.
Run deployPipeline1 without modifying the items in Workspace2.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Run deployPipeline1 without modifying the items in Workspace2.

Detailed analysis for the correct option

Why "Run deployPipeline1 without modifying the items" is correct: In Fabric deployment pipelines, the platform uses "pairing" to know what to do with an item. When an item in the source is paired with its "corresponding item" in the target, the default action on deployment is to overwrite it. Since the question statement confirms that items with the same name are already paired, simply running the pipeline will meet the requirement to overwrite them automatically. Items that are not paired (such as Notebook1) will simply be deployed as new items (clean deploy). Doing this without touching anything in the target environment is the exact definition of "minimize administrative effort".

  • Official documentation: The deployment process: Pairing and overwriting items - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Rename each item in Workspace2 to have the same name as the items in Workspace1: Renaming manually requires development effort and administrative intervention, which contradicts the main requirement to "minimize administrative effort". In addition, the question statement does not require that unpaired items be overwritten, only the "corresponding" (already paired) ones.

  • Official documentation: Managing pipelines with minimal effort - Microsoft Fabric

A. Delete all the items in Workspace2, and then run deployPipeline1: Manually deleting the target environment implies a very high operational effort. It would also destroy the data stored in Lakehouse2 and break local dependencies, which is not a recommended practice in a CI/CD flow where the goal is to overwrite and update metadata, not to delete the environment.

  • Official documentation: Impact of deleting linked items - Microsoft Fabric

C. Back up the items in Workspace2, and then run deployPipeline1: Although backups can be useful, doing so manually before each run adds bureaucratic steps and manual effort that the native tool is designed to avoid. The pipeline by itself already handles overwriting safely.

  • Official documentation: Best practices for deployment - Microsoft Fabric

links.t: The deployment process: Pairing and overwriting items - Microsoft Fabric
Managing pipelines with minimal effort - Microsoft Fabric

q032.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a data pipeline named Pipeline1 and a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

You have a deployment pipeline named deployPipeline1 that deploys Workspace1 to Workspace2.

You restructure Workspace1 by adding a folder named Folder1 and moving Pipeline1 to Folder1.

You use deployPipeline1 to deploy Workspace1 to Workspace2.

What occurs to Workspace2?
options: Folder1 is created, Pipeline1 moves to Folder1, and Lakehouse1 is deployed.
Only Pipeline1 and Lakehouse1 are deployed.
Folder1 is created, and Pipeline1 and Lakehouse1 move to Folder1.
Only Folder1 is created and Pipeline1 moves to Folder1.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Folder1 is created, Pipeline1 moves to Folder1, and Lakehouse1 is deployed.

Detailed analysis for the correct option

Why "Folder1 is created, Pipeline1 moves to Folder1, and Lakehouse1 is deployed" is correct: Deployment pipelines in Microsoft Fabric natively support mirroring the folder structure between environments. When you change the hierarchy in the source (Workspace1) by moving an item into a folder and then deploy the workspace, the deployment pipeline necessarily syncs that structure to the target (Workspace2). The engine's behavior will be as follows:

  1. It will identify that Pipeline1 is now housed in Folder1.

  2. Because a folder is deployed automatically if at least one of its inner items is deployed, it will create Folder1 in Workspace2.

  3. It will move (and update) Pipeline1 into that folder in the target.

  4. Finally, since the question statement directly says "You use deployPipeline1 to deploy Workspace1" (which implies a general deployment of the stage and not a selective deployment of a single file), the other items belonging to that stage, such as Lakehouse1, will be part of the execution batch and will also be deployed in their original location.

  • Official documentation: Deployment rules for workspaces that contain folders - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Why the other options are incorrect:

B. Only Pipeline1 and Lakehouse1 are deployed: This option is incorrect because it wrongly assumes that Fabric deployment pipelines ignore folders (as if they were a flat view without metadata). The folder hierarchy is metadata that is faithfully copied during the deployment of the items they contain.

  • Official documentation: Pairing process and folder hierarchy - Microsoft Fabric

C. Folder1 is created, and Pipeline1 and Lakehouse1 move to Folder1: The Fabric engine strictly respects the location in the source. Since Lakehouse1 was not moved to Folder1 in the development environment (Workspace1), there is no logical instruction for the pipeline to move it in Workspace2. It will remain in the root directory.

  • Official documentation: Item pairing paths - Microsoft Fabric

D. Only Folder1 is created and Pipeline1 moves to Folder1: This option would be correct only if you had used the Selective deployment feature, manually selecting only the pipeline. However, since the case says the entire workspace is deployed, the rest of the items (Lakehouse1) are also involved in the execution cycle and are deployed to guarantee environment parity.

  • Official documentation: Deploying all the content of a stage - Microsoft Fabric

Pairing process and folder hierarchy - Microsoft Fabric
Item pairing paths - Microsoft Fabric

q033.stem:
DRAG DROP -

Your company has a team of developers. The team creates Python libraries of reusable code that is used to transform data.

You create a Fabric workspace name Workspace1 that will be used to develop extract, transform, and load (ETL) solutions by using notebooks.

You need to ensure that the libraries are available by default to new notebooks in Workspace1.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: Create an environment.

  • Step 2: Install the libraries.

  • Step 3: Set the default environment.

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Why this sequence is correct: In Microsoft Fabric, the management of dependencies and custom libraries for Apache Spark workloads (such as notebooks and job definitions) is centralized through an item called an environment. To meet the requirement that internally developed Python libraries be automatically available in all new notebooks in the workspace, this strict logical flow must be followed:

  1. Create an environment: First, you must create the container item, that is, the Fabric environment within the workspace. This item will act as the capsule where the dependencies will be configured.

  2. Install the libraries: Once the environment is created, you must open it, upload the custom library files (usually .whl or .tar.gz files created by the developers) in the "Custom libraries" section, and publish the environment. This packages the libraries so that the Spark cluster installs them at startup.

  3. Set the default environment: Finally, to guarantee that new notebooks use these libraries without the user having to configure it manually each time, you must go to Workspace settings -> Data Engineering/Data Science -> Spark settings, and set this new environment as the default environment of Workspace1.

  • Official documentation: Create and manage environments in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Fabric and Manage libraries for Apache Spark - Microsoft Fabric

Why the other options are incorrect:

Create a pool (Create a Spark pool): In Fabric, it is not strictly necessary to create a custom Spark pool just to install libraries. You can apply an environment with custom libraries directly on the default starter pool. Pool creation focuses on managing compute capacity (autoscale, number of nodes), not on managing code dependencies.

  • Official documentation: Configure Spark pools in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Fabric

Change the runtime version (Change the runtime version): Changing the Spark runtime (for example, going from Runtime 1.1 to 1.2) is used to update the base versions of the Apache Spark engine (e.g., Spark 3.3 to 3.4) and the libraries natively preinstalled by Microsoft. However, it will not install the reusable-code Python libraries developed internally by your team, which requires uploading them manually to an environment.

  • Official documentation: Apache Spark runtimes in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Fabric

q034.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a lakehouse and a notebook named Notebook1. Notebook1 reads data into a DataFrame from a table named Table1 and applies transformation logic. The data from the DataFrame is then written to a new Delta table named Table2 by using a merge operation.

You need to consolidate the underlying Parquet files in Table1.

Which command should you run?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: OPTIMIZE

Detailed analysis for the correct option

Why "OPTIMIZE" is correct: In the Delta Lake format (the default storage architecture for tables in Microsoft Fabric), the OPTIMIZE command is designed natively for exactly this purpose: consolidating and compacting small files. During data transformation and write operations, hundreds or thousands of small Parquet files are often generated, which degrades read performance (the engine wastes time opening and closing file metadata). When you run OPTIMIZE table_name, the Spark engine reads those small files and rewrites them into larger, more efficient Parquet files (the engine's default target is usually around 1 GB per file), drastically improving the speed of future queries.

  • Official documentation: Lakehouse table maintenance (Optimize Delta tables) - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Option A: VACUUM Why it is incorrect: This is the most common confusion error in this domain. The VACUUM command does not alter the structure or size of, nor consolidate, the files that make up the current version of the table. Its sole purpose is garbage collection. When Delta Lake overwrites or deletes data, the original physical Parquet files are not deleted from disk immediately (to allow "time travel"). VACUUM is responsible for physically removing from storage (GCS, S3, or OneLake) those orphaned files that are no longer referenced by the current version of the transaction log and that have exceeded the configured retention period. It frees up space, but does not compact the live table.

  • Official documentation: Removing old files with VACUUM - Microsoft Learn

Option B: BROADCAST Why it is incorrect: BROADCAST is not a storage or table maintenance command. It is a hint, or in-memory execution optimization technique, specific to the Apache Spark engine. It is used during table joins (JOINs) to force the engine to copy an entire small table to the memory of all worker nodes, thus avoiding costly data shuffling across the network. It has no impact on, or relation to, the physical structure of the Parquet files in the data lake.

  • Official documentation: Optimizing joins with Broadcast in Apache Spark - Microsoft Learn

Option D: CACHE Why it is incorrect: The CACHE command (or df.cache()) operates purely at the compute session level. Its function is to materialize and pin the results of a DataFrame in the RAM of the Spark cluster nodes (or in temporary local SSD storage if it does not fit) to speed up subsequent reads within the same notebook process. It is a volatile operation that disappears when the cluster shuts down. It does not perform any modification, write or consolidation on the persistent Parquet files that reside in the OneLake storage layer (Table1).

  • Official documentation: Caching DataFrames in Spark - Microsoft Learn

q035.stem:
You have five Fabric workspaces.

You are monitoring the execution of items by using Monitoring hub.

You need to identify in which workspace a specific item runs.

Which column should you view in Monitoring hub?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option G: Location

Detailed analysis for the correct option

Why "Location" is correct: The Microsoft Fabric monitoring hub is a centralized pane designed to provide visibility into the background activities of all the items a user has access to in their organization. Because it aggregates metrics from multiple workspaces simultaneously, it needs a way to indicate which environment each run belongs to. In the monitoring hub's graphical interface, the Location column is the one that specifically shows the name of the workspace where the item resides and is running.

  • Official documentation: Use the monitoring hub (Interface columns) - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Start time: This column records the exact moment (timestamp) at which the activity entered the queue or began running, but it provides no context about its logical location.

  • Official documentation: Monitoring hub columns (Start time) - Microsoft Fabric

B. Capacity: It shows the identifier of the compute capacity (for example, an F64 capacity) to which the run is being billed. Since a single Fabric capacity can back dozens or hundreds of different workspaces, this column cannot uniquely identify which workspace the item is in.

  • Official documentation: Monitoring hub columns (Capacity) - Microsoft Fabric

C. Activity name: It simply shows the name of the item being run (for example, "Sales_Transformation"), but it lacks the path or the environment where it resides.

  • Official documentation: Monitoring hub columns (Item name) - Microsoft Fabric

D. Submitter: It identifies the user, service principal or system process that triggered the start of the job run.

  • Official documentation: Monitoring hub columns (Submitter) - Microsoft Fabric

E. Item type: It classifies the run by the type of the source item in Fabric, showing labels such as "Data pipeline", "Notebook" or "Dataflow Gen2".

  • Official documentation: Monitoring hub columns (Item type) - Microsoft Fabric

F. Job type: It indicates the nature of the trigger that started the activity. It generally shows whether it was a "Scheduled" run, triggered by the system clock, or an "On-demand" run, forced manually by a user.

  • Official documentation: Monitoring hub columns (Job type) - Microsoft Fabric

q036.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a warehouse named DW1. DW1 is loaded by using a notebook named Notebook1.

You need to identify which version of Delta was used when Notebook1 was executed.

What should you use?
options: the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Fabric Monitor (Monitoring hub)

Detailed analysis for the correct option

Why Fabric Monitor is correct: The Microsoft Fabric monitoring hub is the centralized tool where you can audit and review the history of recent item runs. When you click the specific run of a notebook in this pane, the Details screen shows a section called Runtime information. This is exactly where the platform exposes which Runtime version was used (for example, Runtime 1.3), explicitly breaking down the Apache Spark version (e.g., 3.5) and the Delta Lake version (e.g., 3.2) that the engine used during that run.

  • Official documentation: Contextual monitoring and debugging of notebooks - Microsoft Fabric
answer.incorrect:
Why the other options are incorrect:

A. Real-Time hub: It is the central Fabric pane dedicated exclusively to the ingestion, routing and processing of real-time (streaming) data flows and continuous events. It does not audit past batch runs or track Spark component versions.

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric Real-Time hub - Microsoft Fabric

B. OneLake data hub: It acts as a central catalog or explorer. Its function is to let users discover, share and connect to the different data items in the organization (such as databases or reports), not to inspect code execution logs.

  • Official documentation: Discover data items in the OneLake data hub - Microsoft Fabric

C. the Admin monitoring workspace: This system-generated workspace hosts global tenant-level reports on feature usage and adoption. It is an executive/administrative view, so it does not drop down to the granular technical level of showing the Delta or Spark versions of a particular notebook.

  • Official documentation: What is the admin monitoring workspace - Microsoft Fabric

E. the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app: This app (Metrics app) is designed purely for financial and performance control of capacity (capacity units). It is used to detect consumption spikes, overloads and resource bottlenecks, but it entirely lacks metadata about the source code, libraries or engine versions used in the workloads.

  • Official documentation: Use the Capacity Metrics app - Microsoft Fabric

q037.stem:
DRAG DROP -

You have a Fabric workspace that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

In Warehouse1, you create a table named DimCustomer by running the following statement.

You need to set the Customerkey column as a primary key of the DimCustomer table.

Which three code segments should you run in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate code segments from the list of code segments to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Step 1: ALTER TABLE dbo.DimCustomer

  • Step 2: ADD CONSTRAINT PK_DimCustomer PRIMARY KEY NONCLUSTERED (CustomerKey)

  • Step 3: NOT ENFORCED

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Step 1: ALTER TABLE dbo.DimCustomer. Why it is correct: Since the table was already created by the script in the first image, you must use the T-SQL ALTER TABLE statement to modify its structure and add new constraints. Fabric supports this standard DDL (Data Definition Language) operation within its T-SQL surface area.

  • Official documentation: T-SQL surface area (ALTER TABLE support) - Microsoft Fabric

Step 2: ADD CONSTRAINT PK_DimCustomer PRIMARY KEY NONCLUSTERED (CustomerKey). Why it is correct: In Fabric, data is stored in Delta Parquet, a columnar storage format. Clustered indexes (CLUSTERED), which physically order the data rows on disk based on the key, make no sense and are not supported in this architecture. Therefore, the primary key must necessarily be defined as NONCLUSTERED.

  • Official documentation: Key constraints in Fabric (NONCLUSTERED-only support) - Microsoft Fabric

Step 3: NOT ENFORCED. Why it is correct: This is the most important architectural constraint in Fabric. The data warehouse SQL engine does not validate data uniqueness during insert (INSERT) operations, so as not to penalize bulk data ingestion performance. The responsibility for ensuring there are no duplicates falls on the ETL pipeline. However, declaring the primary key as NOT ENFORCED is vital, because the SQL query optimizer uses this metadata to generate much more efficient execution plans (especially in JOIN operations).

  • Official documentation: Key constraints in Fabric (Metadata usage and NOT ENFORCED) - Microsoft Fabric

Why the other code segments are incorrect:

DROP CONSTRAINT PK_DimCustomer: This standard T-SQL command is used exclusively to remove a constraint that already exists on a table. The scenario statement explicitly asks to "establish" (create or add) a primary key for the first time, not to delete it.

  • Official documentation: ALTER TABLE (Transact-SQL) - Drop constraints

ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED (CustomerKey): In the Microsoft Fabric data warehouse architecture, clustered indexes (CLUSTERED) are not supported. This is because Fabric natively stores data in the Delta Parquet columnar format. A clustered index alters the physical order of the rows on disk based on the key, a concept that is completely incompatible with the immutable structure of Parquet files. Trying to use CLUSTERED will generate a syntax error in Fabric.

  • Official documentation: Key constraints in Fabric (Limitations: CLUSTERED is not supported) - Microsoft Fabric

ENFORCED: The Microsoft Fabric data warehouse engine does not support strict enforcement (ENFORCED) of integrity constraints (such as validating that no duplicates are inserted when loading data). This is by design, to avoid performance bottlenecks during bulk data ingestion. If NOT ENFORCED is not explicitly specified when creating the key, the statement will fail.

  • Official documentation: Constraints in Fabric (Strict NOT ENFORCED requirement) - Microsoft Fabric

q038.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a semantic model named Model1.

You need to dynamically execute and monitor the refresh progress of Model1.

What should you use?
options: dynamic management views in Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
dynamic management views in Azure Data Studio
a semantic link in a notebook

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: a semantic link in a notebook

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Step 1: Why "a semantic link in a notebook" is correct: In Microsoft Fabric, the semantic link feature provides the sempy Python library, which lets you interact programmatically with Power BI semantic models directly from a notebook. This option is the only one that meets both requirements of the question (run and monitor):

  1. Run: You can trigger the refresh dynamically through code by using the sempy.fabric.refresh_dataset() function.

  2. Monitor: Within the same block of code (for example, in a while loop), you can use the sempy.fabric.get_refresh_execution_details() function to continuously and dynamically query the real-time status and progress of that same refresh until it finishes.

  • Official documentation: sempy.fabric.semantic_model package (running and monitoring refreshes) - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Create a shortcut and ensure that caching is disabled for the workspace.
Create a workspace identity and use the identity in a data pipeline.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Create a shortcut and ensure that caching is enabled for the workspace.

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Step 1: Using OneLake shortcuts to avoid data duplication: The scenario explicitly requires avoiding storing a copy of the raw Amazon S3 data in the lakehouses. The shortcuts feature in OneLake lets you connect externally stored data in Amazon S3 virtually and transparently, without having to physically move or duplicate the files into Fabric's internal storage, directly meeting this architectural constraint of the case study.

  • Official documentation: OneLake shortcuts in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Step 2: Enabling caching to minimize egress costs: To meet the requirement of minimizing the egress costs associated with cross-cloud data access between Azure and AWS, it is essential to enable OneLake caching for shortcuts. With caching enabled, repeated reads of the Parquet files stored in S3 are served from the local OneLake cache, avoiding multiple data transfer requests over the cross-cloud network and drastically reducing AWS egress costs.

  • Official documentation: Cache settings for OneLake shortcuts - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Option A: Create a workspace identity and enable high concurrency for the notebooks.

Why it is incorrect: Workspace identities and high concurrency for notebooks are geared toward secure authentication of managed services and parallel execution in Spark, but they provide no mechanism to connect external Amazon S3 storage or to address cross-cloud data transfer costs.

  • Official documentation: Workspace identity in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Option B: Create a shortcut and ensure that caching is disabled for the workspace.

Why it is incorrect: Although creating the shortcut meets the part about not duplicating the raw data, disabling caching would force every query or read of the Parquet files in S3 to make a full network call across the AWS cloud. This would maximize egress costs for every access, directly violating the explicit technical requirement to minimize those costs.

  • Official documentation: Performance and cost considerations for external shortcuts - Microsoft Learn

HOTSPOT -

You need to create the product dimension.

How should you complete the Apache Spark SQL code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

Box 1: INNER JOIN
Box 2: INNER JOIN
Box 3: IsActive = 1;

Detailed analysis of the correct options

Box 1 & Box 2: INNER JOIN Why they are correct: The case study states as a fundamental transformation requirement that: "Some product categories and subcategories are NOT assigned to any product. They are NOT relevant analytically and must be omitted from the product dimension in the gold layer". In dimensional modeling, when a snowflake hierarchy (Product -> Subcategory -> Category) is flattened into a star dimension table (gold layer), using INNER JOIN guarantees a strict intersection. This means that any record in the subcategory or category tables that has no direct match with an existing product (orphan records) will be automatically excluded from the result, perfectly meeting the business requirement with the cleanest possible code.

  • Official documentation: JOIN syntax in Apache Spark SQL - Microsoft Learn

Box 3: IsActive = 1; Why it is correct: In the Data transformation section, the case study literally requires: "The product dimension in the gold layer must include only active products from the product list. Active products are identified by an IsActive value of 1". The WHERE IsActive = 1 clause applies exactly this scalar filter before materializing the resulting DataFrame into the final gold layer Delta table.

  • Official documentation: Implement medallion architecture (gold layer) in Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Incorrect options for Box 1 & Box 2 (Join types):

Option: LEFT OUTER JOIN Why it is incorrect: Applying a LEFT OUTER JOIN would keep all the records of the left table (Products). Although this does not discard products, if the model allowed products without a subcategory, they would end up with NULL values. More critically, if it were used in the second box (Subcategories to Categories), it could compromise dimensional cleanliness. INNER JOIN is the recommended standard practice to guarantee full data quality in the gold dimension according to the specified rules.

  • Official documentation: Dimensional modeling considerations in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Options: FULL JOIN / OUTER JOIN Why they are incorrect: A full or outer join retains all the records of both joined tables, regardless of whether there is a match on the join keys. This would massively insert into the final gold table all of those orphan categories and subcategories that the case study explicitly orders to be omitted.

  • Official documentation: Join operations and their performance impact - Microsoft Learn

Option: LEFT ANTI JOIN Why it is incorrect: ANTI JOIN works as an exclusion filter. It would return only the products that have no associated subcategory. This would completely destroy the dimension table, since it would discard all the valid relational data and keep only the anomalies.

  • Official documentation: Supported JOIN types in Spark SQL - Microsoft Learn

Incorrect options for Box 3 (WHERE clause):

Option: IsActive is not null; Why it is incorrect: Filtering by "not null" would clean out missing data, but it would include inactive products (for example, those where IsActive = 0). This flatly violates the business rule that requires loading only active products into the gold layer.

  • Official documentation: Filtering DataFrames and WHERE syntax in Spark - Microsoft Learn

Options: CategoryName is not null; / SubCategoryName is not null; / ProductNumber is not null; Why they are incorrect: Trying to clean up orphan categories by forcing a filter on null columns in the WHERE clause is a redundant and poor solution. The INNER JOIN configured in boxes 1 and 2 already prevents nulls from appearing due to lack of a match. Furthermore, choosing any of these options would leave out the mandatory IsActive = 1 filter, ruining the main requirement of the dimension.

  • Official documentation: Query optimization and logical filtering in a data lake - Microsoft Learn

q046.stem:
HOTSPOT -

You have a Fabric workspace that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains the following tables and columns.

You need to denormalize the tables and include the ContractType and StartDate columns in the Employee table. The solution must meet the following requirements:

Ensure that the StartDate column is of the date data type.

Ensure that all the rows from the Employee table are preserved and include any matching rows from the Contract table.

Ensure that the result set displays the total number of employees per contract type for all the contract types that have more than two employees.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

Drop-down 1: CONVERT
Drop-down 2: LEFT OUTER JOIN
Drop-down 3: HAVING

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Drop-down 1: CONVERT Why it is correct: The first requirement demands that the StartDate column be of the date data type. In T-SQL, to change the data type of an expression using the comma-separated syntax shown in the image (data_type, expression), the required function is CONVERT. The snippet will read CONVERT(date, c.StartDate), which will transform the original Datetime2 value into a date-only format, meeting both the syntax and business requirements.

  • Official documentation: CAST and CONVERT functions (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 2: LEFT OUTER JOIN Why it is correct: The second requirement literally asks: "Ensure that all rows from the Employee table are retained and include any matching rows from the Contract table". Since the Employee table is declared first in the FROM clause (it is the left table), the only way to guarantee that no employee is lost even if they have no assigned contract is to use a LEFT OUTER JOIN (or LEFT JOIN).

  • Official documentation: Outer joins (LEFT OUTER JOIN) - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 3: HAVING Why it is correct: The third requirement demands filtering the grouped results "for all contract types that have more than two employees". The query calculates this by using an aggregate function: COUNT(DISTINCT EmployeeID). In standard SQL, aggregate functions cannot be used within a WHERE clause. To filter the results after a GROUP BY has been applied, based on the result of an aggregation, the use of the HAVING clause is strictly mandatory.

  • Official documentation: HAVING clause (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Drop-down 1 - Conversion and string functions:

CAST: Why it is incorrect: Although CAST also serves to change data types, its standard syntax requires the AS keyword. The correct syntax would be CAST(c.StartDate AS date). Since the code in the image uses a comma separating the data type and the column, trying to use CAST will produce an immediate syntax error in the SQL engine.

  • Official documentation: Syntax differences between CAST and CONVERT - Microsoft Learn

REPLACE: Why it is incorrect: REPLACE is a text string manipulation function that searches for and replaces specific characters within a string. It has no ability to structurally transform a Datetime2 data type into a Date data type.

  • Official documentation: REPLACE function (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

SUBSTRING: Why it is incorrect: SUBSTRING is another text manipulation function designed to extract a portion of a string based on a start index and a length. It does not perform data type conversions, so using it here would fail both logically and syntactically.

  • Official documentation: SUBSTRING function (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 2 - JOIN types:

CROSS JOIN: Why it is incorrect: A CROSS JOIN generates a Cartesian product, combining every row of the first table with every row of the second. It does not use (or support) an ON clause to match identifiers (EmployeeID = EmployeeID), which would cause a syntax error in this code and wrongly multiply the data.

  • Official documentation: Use cross joins (CROSS JOIN) - Microsoft Learn

INNER JOIN: Why it is incorrect: INNER JOIN returns only the rows that have exact matches in both tables. If it were used, any employee who had no record in the contract table would disappear from the final result, violating the requirement to retain all rows from the Employee table.

  • Official documentation: Inner joins (INNER JOIN) - Microsoft Learn

RIGHT OUTER JOIN: Why it is incorrect: RIGHT OUTER JOIN preserves all rows of the right table (Contract) and only the matching ones from the left (Employee). This would do exactly the opposite of what was requested: it would keep all contracts even if they had no employee, but it would discard employees without a contract.

  • Official documentation: Right outer joins (RIGHT OUTER JOIN) - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 3 - Filtering clauses:

WHERE: Why it is incorrect: The WHERE clause filters rows individually before the data is grouped (GROUP BY). The SQL engine strictly prohibits the use of aggregate functions such as COUNT() inside a WHERE, so this code would fail to compile.

  • Official documentation: Limitations of the WHERE clause with aggregate functions - Microsoft Learn

CONTAINS: Why it is incorrect: CONTAINS is a predicate used exclusively in the SQL Server Full-Text Search engine to search for precise words or phrases in character columns. It is not used to evaluate mathematical operations or grouping filters.

  • Official documentation: CONTAINS predicate (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

LIMIT: Why it is incorrect: First, LIMIT is not a valid clause in standard T-SQL (the T-SQL equivalent is TOP or OFFSET FETCH). Second, even in the SQL dialects that support it (such as MySQL or PostgreSQL), LIMIT serves to restrict the maximum number of rows returned at the end of the query, not to evaluate a greater-than-two logical condition after a grouping.

  • Official documentation: TOP clause (Transact-SQL as an alternative to LIMIT) - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 2: An eventstream processor Why it is correct: The main requirement demands that the filter (City = Kansas) be applied before the data reaches its destination (the lakehouse) and with the minimum development effort. Within a Fabric eventstream, the tool designed for exactly this purpose is the event processor (eventstream processor). It provides a no-code visual editor where you simply drag a Filter transformation node between the source and the destination, achieving the goal directly and natively in the stream.

Drop-down 1 - Data processor:

A data pipeline: Why it is incorrect: Data pipelines in Fabric are designed for orchestration and batch data movement from static stores. They do not have native connectors optimized to subscribe directly to a continuous event stream such as Azure Event Hubs. Using one would require complex configurations (such as reading previously captured files in Blob Storage), which would maximize development effort and break the architecture of the existing eventstream.

  • Official documentation: Copy activity in data pipelines - Microsoft Learn

A Dataflow Gen2 dataflow: Why it is incorrect: Dataflow Gen2 is a powerful Power Query-based engine for batch transformations, but it is not designed to process real-time message queues or continuous streams. Replacing the eventstream with a Dataflow Gen2 dataflow to connect to an event hub would be technically unfeasible and inefficient for this scenario.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to Dataflow Gen2 - Microsoft Learn

An eventstream with a custom endpoint: Why it is incorrect: A custom endpoint is used in an eventstream when you want your own application to send (push) data directly to Microsoft Fabric. In this case, the data already resides in an external Azure service (Azure Event Hubs), so the correct approach is to configure an external source that reads from that service, not to create a custom endpoint.

  • Official documentation: Add a custom app source to an eventstream - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 2 - Filtering:

A Filter activity in a data pipeline: Why it is incorrect: Since the engine that processes the extraction is an eventstream, a data pipeline activity is outside that real-time ecosystem. It cannot intercept or modify the events in transit before the eventstream deposits them in the lakehouse.

  • Official documentation: Filter activity in Azure Data Factory and Fabric - Microsoft Learn

A filter in a Dataflow Gen2 dataflow: Why it is incorrect: As with the data pipeline, Dataflow Gen2 is a separate item that operates in batches. You cannot embed a Dataflow Gen2 Power Query step in the middle of an eventstream's path to filter the events before the destination.

  • Official documentation: Transform data in Dataflow Gen2 - Microsoft Learn

A KQL statement: Why it is incorrect: KQL queries are the ideal tool for applying transformations (such as update policies) when the destination is a KQL database. However, the question clearly specifies that the destination of Eventstream1 is a lakehouse (which stores the data in Delta Parquet format). A lakehouse does not support KQL statements to transform data at ingestion time, so the eventstream's visual processor is the only valid option.

You are building a data loading pattern for Fabric notebook workloads.

You have the following code segment:

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

Statement 1: No
Statement 2: No
Statement 3: Yes

Detailed analysis for each statement

Statement 1: The target table will always be overwritten. Why the answer is No: When analyzing the error-handling structure (try/except) of the Python code provided, the statement that overwrites the table df_source.write.format('delta').mode('overwrite').saveAsTable(...) is located strictly inside the first except block. This means the overwrite will only run conditionally if the initial try block fails, that is, if the target table does not yet exist or cannot be read through DeltaTable.forName. Therefore, it is not always overwritten.

  • Official documentation: Write data to Delta tables (overwrite mode) - Microsoft Learn

Statement 2: The merge operation will always run. Why the answer is No: If you look at the end of the first except block (right after it prints an error or after the nested block ends), there is a return statement. This statement forces an immediate exit from the loading_pattern_sample function. If the table did not exist and the engine runs the initial overwrite, the code reaches that return and ends execution without ever reaching the second try block where the merge operation is defined and run. Therefore, the merge does not always run.

  • Official documentation: Python control flow (return statement) - Python documentation

Statement 3: The loading pattern supports both full and incremental loading requirements. Why the answer is Yes: The code implements a classic design pattern known as "dynamic upsert" for Delta Lake, which handles both scenarios perfectly:

  • Full load: If this is the first time the code runs (the table does not exist), the first block fails and catches the exception, performing an initial full load by saving the whole dataframe as a new table.

  • Incremental load: If the table already exists, the code skips the except block and proceeds to the merge block. There, it evaluates record by record: it inserts the new rows (whenNotMatchedInsertAll) and updates existing rows only if it detects changes in the non-key columns (update_condition). This is the exact definition of an incremental load.

HOTSPOT -

You have a Fabric workspace that contains two lakehouses named Lakehouse1 and Lakehouse2. Lakehouse1 contains staging data in a Delta table named Orderlines. Lakehouse2 contains a Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD)

dimension table named Dim_Customer.

You need to build a query that will combine data from Orderlines and Dim_Customer to create a new fact table named Fact_Orders. The new table must meet the following requirements:

Enable the analysis of customer orders based on historical attributes.

Enable the analysis of customer orders based on the current attributes.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

Drop-down 1: o.OrderDate >= c.valid_from_datetime t (Note: the letter "t" at the end is a standard typo in the dumps of this exam, but the relational logic is correct).
Drop-down 2: o.OrderDate < c.valid_to_datetime

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Drop-downs 1 and 2: Point-in-time join logic for SCD Type 2 Why it is correct: In dimensional modeling, a Type 2 slowly changing dimension (SCD) tracks the history of changes by creating a new row (with a new surrogate key, customer_key) each time a customer attribute changes. Each row has a validity start date (valid_from_datetime) and a validity end date (valid_to_datetime).

To meet the requirement to "Allow analysis of orders based on historical attributes", you must assign each transaction the exact surrogate key that was active at the time the order occurred. This requires evaluating that the order date (OrderDate) is greater than or equal to the date on which the customer record took effect, and strictly less than the date on which that record expired. The required combination is: o.OrderDate >= c.valid_from_datetime AND o.OrderDate < c.valid_to_datetime.

In addition, the SELECT query projects both the surrogate key (c.customer_key) and the business key (c.customer_id). Storing the business key in the fact table is what makes it possible to meet the second requirement: "Allow analysis based on current attributes", since in the downstream semantic model that customer_id can be linked to the dimension row that has the current flag.

  • Official documentation: Dimensional modeling: Type 2 slowly changing dimensions (SCD) - Microsoft Learn and Star schema guidance: SCD Type 2 in Power BI - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Drop-down 1 - Incorrect options:

c.is_current = 1: Why it is incorrect: If you use the current record indicator (is_current = 1) in the join condition (JOIN) when loading the fact table, all orders (regardless of which year they are from) will be linked to the customer's most recent state. This overwrites history and destroys the ability to perform the historical analysis required by the first business requirement.

  • Official documentation: Anti-patterns in handling SCD Type 2 (loss of history) - Microsoft Learn

o.OrderDate > c.valid_to_datetime: Why it is incorrect: This mathematical condition would try to join an order to a customer record that had already expired before the order was placed. It is logically the inverse of the concept of time and would cause orders to find no valid matches or to be associated with incorrect historical profiles.

  • Official documentation: Predicate logic for validity dates - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 2 - Incorrect options:

c.is_current = 1: Why it is incorrect: For the same reason given above. Forcing the join exclusively to the current record breaks the point-in-time matching that defines the purpose of an SCD Type 2 dimension.

  • Official documentation: Dimension modeling (avoid static joins in fact tables) - Microsoft Learn

o.OrderDate <= c.valid_from_datetime: Why it is incorrect: This condition would try to join the transaction to a dimension record that was not yet valid at the time the order occurred (that is, the record took effect after the purchase). This breaks temporal causality and corrupts the historical data.

  • Official documentation: Resolving surrogate keys by using dates - Microsoft Learn

q052.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

In an external data source, you have data files that are 500 GB each. A new file is added every day.

You need to ingest the data into Lakehouse1 without applying any transformations. The solution must meet the following requirements Trigger the process when a new file is added.

Provide the highest throughput.

Which type of item should you use to ingest the data?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option D: Data pipeline

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Data pipeline: Why it is correct: This option perfectly meets the three fundamental requirements of the scenario:

  1. Highest performance for massive files: The 500 GB files are extremely large. In Fabric, data pipelines use the Copy data activity, which has a massive, scalable, parallelized data movement engine, offering the highest possible bandwidth and throughput for static ingestions of this size.

  2. Event-based trigger: Data pipelines support storage event triggers. This allows the pipeline to run automatically at the exact moment the creation or arrival of a new file in the source is detected.

  3. No transformations: The Copy data activity performs a literal byte-for-byte (or schema-to-schema) copy without applying heavy computational transformations, making it the ideal tool for "raw" loads.

  • Official documentation: Copy activity in data pipelines (bulk performance) - Microsoft Learn and Storage event triggers in Data Factory - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Dataflow Gen2: Why it is incorrect: Although a Dataflow Gen2 can move data, its engine (based on Power Query) is designed and optimized specifically for applying complex row-by-row transformations. For a static 500 GB file that requires no transformation, Dataflow Gen2 would incur an enormous memory and processing time overhead, delivering far lower performance than the copy activity of a data pipeline. Furthermore, it has no independent native event trigger; it would require a data pipeline to orchestrate it.

  • Official documentation: Differences between Dataflows Gen2 and data pipelines - Microsoft Learn

Eventstream: Why it is incorrect: Eventstreams are designed to ingest a continuous flow of small messages or real-time telemetry (for example, millions of JSON records of a few kilobytes per second coming from IoT sensors). They are neither designed for nor support the bulk transfer of massive 500 GB static files.

  • Official documentation: Introduction to Microsoft Fabric eventstreams - Microsoft Learn

Streaming dataset: Why it is incorrect: As discussed in previous questions, a streaming dataset is a Power BI item designed to "push" small batches of data directly to a real-time visual dashboard. It has nothing to do with ingesting bulk files into a lakehouse, nor the capacity to handle 500 GB volumes.

  • Official documentation: Real-time streaming in Power BI - Microsoft Learn

You have a Fabric workspace that contains an eventhouse and a KQL database named Database1. Database1 has the following:

A table named Table1 -

A table named Table2 -

An update policy named Policy1 -

Policy1 sends data from Table1 to Table2.

Recently, the following actions were performed on Table1:

An additional element named temperature was added to the StreamData column.

The data type of the Timestamp column was changed to date.

The data type of the DeviceId column was changed to string.

You plan to load additional records to Table2.

Which two records will load from Table1 to Table2? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

A)

(Correct Answer)

B)

C)

(Correct Answer)

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: The image record (Date 2024-05-18, with valid GUID and temperature).

  • Option D: The image record (Date 2024-05-24, with valid GUID without temperature).

Detailed analysis of the correct options

Why they are correct: The update policy will try to convert (cast) the text string in Table 1 to the guid type required by Table 2. The KQL engine can convert a string to guid only if it has the exact valid hexadecimal format (8-4-4-4-12 characters). These two images are the only ones that have a DeviceId in the correct format (81416f30-60a2-4e75-9b19-2a84ea059735). The other two changes mentioned in the scenario do not prevent the load: the date data type is automatically converted to datetime (adding the hours as zero) and the dynamic column accepts any variation in the JSON schema, so whether or not the temperature node is present is irrelevant.

  • Official documentation: The guid data type in Kusto (KQL) - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Record B. Why it is incorrect: This record tries to send the string "81416f30" to the DeviceId column of Table 2. Because it has only 8 characters, it does not meet the mandatory structure of a GUID. The type conversion will fail while the update policy runs and the record will not be loaded.

Record C Why it is incorrect: This record tries to insert a string that is too long (more than 32 characters) and that also contains letters that do not belong to the hexadecimal system (such as h, y, t). It is mathematically impossible to parse this string as a valid guid type, which causes the record to fail at the destination.

You have a Fabric workspace.

You are debugging a statement and discover the following issues:

Sometimes, the statement fails to return all the expected rows.

The PurchaseDate output column is NOT in the expected format of mmm dd, yy.

You need to resolve the issues. The solution must ensure that the data types of the results are retained. The results can contain blank cells.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.
