answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Dropdown 1: ,try_cast(item_name as varchar(20))

  • Dropdown 2: ,convert(varchar, purchase_date, 7)

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Dropdown 1: ,try_cast(item_name as varchar(20)) Why it is correct: The scenario describes that the query "does not return all the expected rows" and warns that "the results may contain blank cells". This is the classic behavior of a runtime conversion error: if you use a standard conversion function and a single record fails to convert, the SQL engine raises an error and abruptly stops the execution of the query, truncating the result set. The TRY_CAST function solves this natively by evaluating each row safely. If the conversion fails, instead of aborting the query, it returns a NULL value (the blank cell the business requires), guaranteeing that absolutely all the rows of the base table are returned.

  • Official documentation: TRY_CAST (Transact-SQL) function - Microsoft Learn

Dropdown 2: ,convert(varchar, purchase_date, 7) Why it is correct: The requirement demands explicitly formatting the date column to the display format mmm dd, yy (for example, Jan 01, 24). In T-SQL, the CONVERT function accepts a third numeric argument (the style code) to determine the output format of dates as text strings. Style code 7 corresponds exactly to the Mon dd, yy standard.

  • Official documentation: Date format styles in CAST and CONVERT - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Dropdown 1 - Standard CONVERT functions:

,convert(varchar(20), item_name) / ,convert(varchar(max), item_name): Why they are incorrect: If the table contains anomalous data that cannot be cleanly converted to the configured target type, the traditional CONVERT function will fail fatally. This will throw a runtime exception that interrupts the processing of the batch, causing the exact problem the scenario asks to fix (the loss of returned rows).

  • Official documentation: Error handling in CAST and CONVERT - Microsoft Learn

Dropdown 2 - Style codes 109 and 112:

,convert(varchar, purchase_date, 109): Why it is incorrect: Style code 109 formats the date as mon dd yyyy hh:mi:ss:mmmAM (for example, Jan 1 2024 12:00:00:000AM). It does not meet the short format requirement.

  • Official documentation: Style 109 formats - Microsoft Learn

,convert(varchar, purchase_date, 112): Why it is incorrect: Style code 112 is used to generate compact ISO standard formats without separators, structured as yyyymmdd (for example, 20240101). It is incompatible with the requested format rule.

You are developing a data pipeline named Pipeline1.

You need to add a Copy data activity that will copy data from a Snowflake data source to a Fabric warehouse.

What should you configure?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Enable staging

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Enable staging: Why it is correct: In the architecture of Microsoft Fabric data pipelines (as in Azure Data Factory), the native Snowflake connector is designed to deliver maximum performance by using Snowflake's internal bulk unload and load command. This native extraction command mandatorily requires unloading the data to an intermediate temporary storage location (staging) before moving it to its final destination (in this case, the Fabric warehouse). Therefore, for the Copy data activity to work when Snowflake is the source, it is a strict architectural requirement to turn on the "Enable staging" setting and associate a temporary storage connection with it (such as Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 or Blob Storage).

Degree of copy parallelism: Why it is incorrect: This is an advanced and entirely optional setting within the copy activity. It is used to force or limit the maximum number of simultaneous connections the engine can open against the source database in an attempt to speed up reading. It is not a mandatory functional requirement to connect to and extract data from Snowflake.

  • Official documentation: Copy activity performance features - Microsoft Learn

Fault tolerance: Why it is incorrect: Fault tolerance is an optional quality control feature. It lets you tell the pipeline what to do if it finds incompatible data during the copy (for example, skip the faulty rows so that the process does not fail and keeps running). It has no relationship with the mandatory extraction protocol required by Snowflake.

  • Official documentation: Copy activity fault tolerance - Microsoft Learn

Enable logging: Why it is incorrect: It is a purely operational and optional telemetry setting. It is used to generate an audit file with the detailed log of the files processed or the rows skipped (when combined with fault tolerance). It does not solve the problem of the physical transfer of the data from the source cluster to the destination.

You have a KQL database that contains two tables named Stream and Reference. Stream contains streaming data in the following format.

Reference contains reference data in the following format.

Both tables contain millions of rows.

You have the following KQL queryset.

You need to reduce how long it takes to run the KQL queryset.

Solution: You change the join type to kind=outer.

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option: No

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Why the answer is No: The scenario's goal strictly requires reducing the time the query takes to run. Changing the join type from inner to full outer will achieve exactly the opposite: it will drastically increase the run time and the memory consumption of the cluster.

An inner join processes and returns only the records where the DeviceId matches in both tables. By contrast, an outer join forces the Kusto engine to process, hold in memory and return absolutely all the rows of both tables (which have "millions of rows", according to the case), filling in nulls where there is no match. Besides destroying performance, this solution completely changes the business logic of the original results.

  • Official documentation: The join operator in Kusto Query Language (KQL) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect option

Why the Yes option is incorrect: Selecting "Yes" wrongly assumes that expanding the output data set reduces the processing effort. In distributed systems such as KQL, outer joins are the most expensive relational operation there is.

If the real goal in the exam is to optimize performance when joining a high-volume table (Stream) with a reference data table (Reference), the correct architectural solution would have been to replace the join operator with the lookup operator (which is highly optimized for looking up reference data), or to use broadcast hints in the current join by adding hint.strategy=broadcast. Never change the nature of the join to outer.

  • Official documentation: Best practices for KQL queries (join optimization and the lookup operator) - Microsoft Learn

You have the following KQL queryset.

You need to reduce how long it takes to run the KQL queryset.

Solution: You change project to extend.

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option: No

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Why the answer is No: The scenario's goal is to reduce the time the query takes to run. In Kusto Query Language (KQL), the project operator is used to specifically select which columns to keep in the result, discarding all the others. This is one of the fundamental best practices for optimizing performance, because it drastically reduces the volume of data the engine has to process, hold in memory and transfer.

By contrast, the extend operator calculates and adds new columns, but it keeps absolutely all the original columns of the data set. Changing a project operator to an extend means the engine will stop discarding the unnecessary columns and will carry the full weight of the two original tables (which contain millions of rows) all the way to the end of the execution. This will increase memory consumption and significantly worsen the run time.

  • Official documentation: Best practices for KQL queries (reduce the number of columns) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect option

Why the Yes option is incorrect: Selecting "Yes" wrongly assumes that keeping the original data with extend is a lighter operation than filtering it with project. In Big Data and distributed analytics environments (such as Microsoft Fabric or Azure Data Explorer), carrying unused columns through expensive operations (such as a join of millions of rows) is the most common performance antipattern. The strict architectural rule is to project only the necessary columns as early as possible in the query.

  • Official documentation: The extend operator in KQL (retention of base columns) - Microsoft Learn

The extend operator in KQL (retention of base columns) - Microsoft Learn

q059.stem:
Note: This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals. Some question sets might have more than one correct solution, while others might not have a correct solution.

After you answer a question in this section, you will NOT be able to return to it. As a result, these questions will not appear in the review screen.

You have a KQL database that contains two tables named Stream and Reference. Stream contains streaming data in the following format.

Reference contains reference data in the following format.

Both tables contain millions of rows.

You have the following KQL queryset.

You need to reduce how long it takes to run the KQL queryset.

Solution: You move the filter to line 02.

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option: Yes

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Why the answer is Yes: The main goal of the scenario is to reduce the run time of the query over two tables that contain millions of rows. In Kusto Query Language (KQL), the structural golden rule for performance optimization is to filter early and often. Moving the filter operator (the where clause) to line 02 means applying it immediately after declaring the base table (Stream) and strictly before running the join operation with the Reference table.

By doing this, you massively reduce the volume of data the Kusto engine has to load into memory for the cross relational operation. The join operator is the most resource-intensive statement; if you filter first, the join is performed over an infinitely smaller subset of data, which drastically reduces CPU consumption and total run time. This action flawlessly meets the business goal.

  • Official documentation: Best practices for KQL queries (filter first) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect option

Why the No option is incorrect: Selecting "No" would mean believing that the order of operators does not affect performance in Big Data queries. If the filter is left after the join, the engine is forced to join millions of rows from both tables only to discard most of the results at the end of the process. Running heavy computational work on records that are going to be eliminated anyway is the worst possible performance antipattern in KQL. Placing the filter at the top solves this directly.

  • Official documentation: Optimizing queries by using the where operator before joins - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Best practices for KQL queries (filter first) - Microsoft Learn
Optimizing queries by using the where operator before joins - Microsoft Learn

q060.stem:
Note: This question is part of a series of questions that present the same scenario. Each question in the series contains a unique solution that might meet the stated goals. Some question sets might have more than one correct solution, while others might not have a correct solution.

After you answer a question in this section, you will NOT be able to return to it. As a result, these questions will not appear in the review screen.

You have a KQL database that contains two tables named Stream and Reference. Stream contains streaming data in the following format.

Reference contains reference data in the following format.

Both tables contain millions of rows.

You have the following KQL queryset.

You need to reduce how long it takes to run the KQL queryset.

Solution: You add the make_list() function to the output columns.

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option: No

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Why the answer is No: The scenario's goal strictly requires reducing the time the query takes to run over two tables that contain millions of rows. In Kusto Query Language (KQL), the make_list() function is an aggregation function that collects all the values of an expression within a group and packs them into a dynamic array (a JSON array).

Performing this operation on large data sets is extremely expensive in terms of computation and memory. The cluster has to keep all the values in memory to build the dynamic arrays before it can return the result. Therefore, instead of optimizing the query, adding make_list() will severely increase the run time and latency, and could even cause an error due to excessive memory consumption on the node.

  • Official documentation: The make_list() aggregation function in KQL - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect option

Why the Yes option is incorrect: Selecting "Yes" makes the conceptual mistake of believing that returning fewer rows in the final output (by packing them into lists) reduces the work of the database engine. The effort the engine must make to serialize and build those massive JSON arrays from millions of source records deeply penalizes performance. The real optimization techniques in KQL (as we saw in the previous questions of this series) are to push filters up (where) or to discard unnecessary columns (project), never to add complex aggregations without need.

  • Official documentation: Best practices for KQL queries (memory usage in aggregations) - Microsoft Learn

q061.stem:
HOTSPOT -

You are processing streaming data from an external data provider.

You have the following code segment.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true.

Otherwise, select No.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Statement 1: No

  • Statement 2: Yes

  • Statement 3: Yes

Detailed analysis of each statement

To solve this question, we first have to mentally simulate the sorting and ranking as the KQL engine would.

Step 1: Sorting (sort by Location desc, UnitsSold desc) The engine will sort the cities alphabetically in descending order (Z to A), and then the sales (UnitsSold) from highest to lowest within each city. The resulting order will be:

  1. Washington DC, Contoso, 400

  2. Washington DC, Litware, 300

  3. Seattle, Contoso, 300

  4. Seattle, Litware, 100

  5. Seattle, Fabrikam, 100

  6. San Francisco, Relecloud, 500

  7. San Francisco, Litware, 500

  8. New York, Litware, 1000

  9. New York, Contoso, 300

  10. New York, Relecloud, 300

  11. New York, Fabrikam, 200

Step 2: Ranking (extend Rank=row_rank_dense(UnitsSold, prev(Location) != Location)) The row_rank_dense function assigns a rank (1, 2, 3...) based on the UnitsSold column. The argument prev(Location) != Location tells the engine to reset the counter (go back to 1) every time the city (Location) value changes from the previous row. "Dense" means that if there is a tie in sales, both get the same rank and the next value does not skip numbers. Applying this to the sorted set:

  • Washington DC: Contoso (400) -> Rank 1 | Litware (300) -> Rank 2

  • Seattle: Contoso (300) -> Rank 1 | Litware (100) -> Rank 2 | Fabrikam (100) -> Rank 2 (tie with Litware)

  • San Francisco: Relecloud (500) -> Rank 1 | Litware (500) -> Rank 1 (tie with Relecloud)

  • New York: Litware (1000) -> Rank 1 | Contoso (300) -> Rank 2 | Relecloud (300) -> Rank 2 (tie) | Fabrikam (200) -> Rank 3

  • Therefore the query result would look like this:
    | Washington DC | Contoso | 400 | 1 |
    | Washington DC | Litware | 300 | 2 |
    | Seattle | Contoso | 300 | 1 |
    | Seattle | Litware | 100 | 2 |
    | Seattle | Fabrikam | 100 | 2 |
    | San Francisco | Relecloud | 500 | 1 |
    | San Francisco | Litware | 500 | 1 |
    | New York | Litware | 1000 | 1 |
    | New York | Contoso | 300 | 2 |
    | New York | Relecloud | 300 | 2 |
    | New York | Fabrikam | 200 | 3 |

Now we evaluate the statements:

Statement 1: Litware from New York will be displayed at the top of the result set. Why the answer is No: As we saw in the sorting (sort by Location desc), the letter 'W' of Washington DC comes before the 'N' of New York in descending order. Therefore, the top row of the result will be Contoso from Washington DC, not Litware from New York.

  • Official documentation: The sort operator (KQL) - Microsoft Learn

Statement 2: Fabrikam in Seattle will have value = 2 in the Rank column. Why the answer is Yes: In Seattle, rank 1 is for Contoso (300). Then come Litware (100) and Fabrikam (100). Since both have the same units sold, the row_rank_dense function assigns both rank 2, strictly fulfilling the statement.

  • Official documentation: The row_rank_dense() function in KQL - Microsoft Learn

Statement 3: Litware in San Francisco will have the same value in the Rank column as Litware in New York. Why the answer is Yes:

  • In San Francisco, Litware sold 500 units, tying for first place with Relecloud. Therefore, its Rank is 1.

  • In New York, Litware sold 1000 units, being the absolute leader in that city. Therefore, its Rank is also 1. Both get the value 1, making the statement mathematically correct.

  • Official documentation: Window functions in KQL - Microsoft Learn

links.t: The sort operator (KQL) - Microsoft Learn
The row_rank_dense() function in KQL - Microsoft Learn
Window functions in KQL - Microsoft Learn

q062.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

Lakehouse1 contains a Delta table named Table1.

You analyze Table1 and discover that Table1 contains 2,000 Parquet files of 1 MB each.

You need to minimize how long it takes to query Table1.

What should you do?
options: Disable V-Order and run the OPTIMIZE command.
Disable V-Order and run the VACUUM command.
Run the OPTIMIZE and VACUUM commands.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Run the OPTIMIZE and VACUUM commands.

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Run the OPTIMIZE and VACUUM commands: Why it is correct: The scenario describes 2,000 files of 1 MB. This is the classic bottleneck known as the "small file problem", which severely degrades query performance because the engine spends more time opening files and reading their metadata than processing actual data.

To solve it, you must run the OPTIMIZE command. This command performs a bin-packing process, merging those 2,000 tiny files into a much smaller group of large, efficient files (approaching the optimal size of 1 GB). Afterward, the VACUUM command physically removes from storage the 2,000 original 1 MB files that have been left orphaned and obsolete after the optimization, keeping storage clean and reducing cost.

  • Official documentation: Optimize Delta Lake tables (OPTIMIZE and VACUUM) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Disable V-Order and run the OPTIMIZE / VACUUM command: Why they are incorrect: Both options suggest disabling V-Order, which is counterproductive and will destroy performance. V-Order is a write-time optimization exclusive to Microsoft Fabric that is applied natively to Parquet files to drastically speed up read times in the platform's compute engines (such as Power BI, SQL and Spark). By default, when you run OPTIMIZE in Fabric, the data is rewritten with V-Order applied automatically. Disabling it would go directly against the goal of "minimizing the time it takes to query the table".

Additionally, running only VACUUM without running OPTIMIZE would not solve the initial problem, because VACUUM does not consolidate files; it only removes those that have already been logically marked as deleted.

  • Official documentation: V-Order optimization in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

links.t: Optimize Delta Lake tables (OPTIMIZE and VACUUM) - Microsoft Learn
V-Order optimization in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

q063.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Data is loaded daily into Warehouse1 by using data pipelines and stored procedures.

You discover that the daily data load takes longer than expected.

You need to monitor Warehouse1 to identify the names of users that are actively running queries.

Which view should you use?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option E: sys.dm_exec_sessions

Detailed analysis of the correct option

sys.dm_exec_sessions: Why it is correct: The key requirement of the scenario is to identify the names of the users who are consuming warehouse resources in real time. In the ecosystem of T-SQL dynamic management views (DMVs) supported by Microsoft Fabric, the sys.dm_exec_sessions view is the only one that contains the authentication and identity information. Specifically, it stores the login_name column, which tells you exactly who is connected. By filtering this view by its status column (status = 'running'), you can directly and instantly see which users are actively running queries in the warehouse at that precise moment.

  • Official documentation: sys.dm_exec_sessions (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

sys.dm_exec_requests: Why it is incorrect: This is the main "trap" option in this type of question. Although this view is perfect for seeing the technical details of what is actively running at that moment (the query itself, CPU time, blocking), it does not contain the user name. It only records the session identifier (session_id). To get the name, you would necessarily have to join this view with sys.dm_exec_sessions. On its own, it does not meet the goal of showing who is running it.

  • Official documentation: sys.dm_exec_requests (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

sys.dm_exec_connections: Why it is incorrect: This view returns information about the physical and network properties of the connection (such as the client IP address, the network protocol or the connection time). It does not contain the user identity (login_name) nor does it report whether a query is actively running on that connection at that moment.

  • Official documentation: sys.dm_exec_connections (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

queryinsights.long_running_queries / queryinsights.frequently_run_queries: Why they are incorrect: These two options are part of the Query Insights feature in Fabric. They are analytical views that collect and aggregate execution history over time to help you identify trends (which queries have historically been the slowest or the most frequently run). They are not real-time views for monitoring the current active sessions, nor are they designed for live monitoring (real-time troubleshooting).

  • Official documentation: Query insights in Fabric data warehousing - Microsoft Learn

links.t: sys.dm_exec_sessions (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn
sys.dm_exec_requests (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn
sys.dm_exec_connections (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn
Query insights in Fabric data warehousing - Microsoft Learn

q064.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains an eventstream named EventStream1. EventStream1 outputs events to a table in a lakehouse.

You need to remove files that are older than seven days and are no longer in use.

Which command should you run?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option: VACUUM

Detailed analysis of the correct option

VACUUM (the VACUUM command): Why it is correct: In the Delta Lake architecture (the format underlying lakehouses in Fabric), when data is updated, deleted or optimized, the underlying physical files (Parquet) are not deleted immediately. This is done on purpose to enable the "time travel" feature, which lets you query previous versions of the table. The VACUUM command is the tool specifically designed to clean up storage: it scans the transaction log and physically removes all files that are no longer referenced by the active table and that are older than the configured retention period. By default, this VACUUM retention period is exactly 7 days, perfectly meeting the scenario's requirement.

  • Official documentation: The VACUUM command in Delta Lake - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

OPTIMIZE (the OPTIMIZE command): Why it is incorrect: As we saw in previous questions, the OPTIMIZE command is used exclusively to consolidate small files into larger files to improve read performance (bin-packing). However, OPTIMIZE does not delete the original small files; it simply creates new consolidated files and unlinks the old ones from the transaction log. To actually delete those old files from storage after an OPTIMIZE, you must run VACUUM.

  • Official documentation: Optimize Delta Lake tables (OPTIMIZE) - Microsoft Learn

COMPUTE (the COMPUTE command): Why it is incorrect: COMPUTE-type commands (such as COMPUTE STATS in some database engines) are used to collect and calculate statistics about the data in a table (value distribution, row count) to help the query optimizer generate better execution plans. They have absolutely no function related to the physical deletion of files or storage maintenance.

  • Official documentation: Statistics in Fabric data warehousing - Microsoft Learn

CLONE: Why it is incorrect: The CLONE command in Delta Lake is used to create an exact copy of an existing table at a specific point in time (either a deep clone that copies the physical data, or a shallow clone that copies only the metadata). Its purpose is environment replication, testing or backups, not the cleanup and deletion of expired files.

  • Official documentation: Clone tables in Delta Lake - Microsoft Learn

links.t: The VACUUM command in Delta Lake - Microsoft Learn
Optimize Delta Lake tables (OPTIMIZE) - Microsoft Learn
Statistics in Fabric data warehousing - Microsoft Learn
Clone tables in Delta Lake - Microsoft Learn

q065.stem:
You have a Fabric warehouse named DW1 that loads data by using a data pipeline named Pipeline1. Pipeline1 uses a Copy data activity with a dynamic SQL source. Pipeline1 is scheduled to run every 15 minutes.

You discover that Pipeline1 keeps failing.

You need to identify which SQL query was executed when the pipeline failed.

What should you do?
options: From Monitoring hub, select the latest failed run of Pipeline1, and then view the output JSON.
From Monitoring hub, select the latest failed run of Pipeline1, and then view the input JSON.
From Real-time hub, select Fabric events, and then review the details of Microsoft.Fabric.ItemReadFailed.
From Real-time hub, select Fabric events, and then review the details of Microsoft. Fabric.ItemUpdateFailed.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option B: From Monitoring hub, select the latest failed run of Pipeline1, and then view the input JSON.

Detailed analysis of the correct option

From Monitoring hub, select the latest failed run of Pipeline1, and then view the input JSON: Why it is correct: In Microsoft Fabric data pipelines (which share their architecture with Azure Data Factory), when you use dynamic content to generate parameters (such as a dynamic SQL query in a copy activity), the engine evaluates that expression right before the activity starts running. The exact result of that evaluation is what is injected into the activity. This entire pre-execution configuration package is recorded in the input JSON. Therefore, by reviewing the input JSON of the failed activity in the Monitoring hub, you will see the final, fully resolved SQL query that the engine tried to run against the database, which lets you debug exactly what failed in the generated code.

  • Official documentation: Monitor data pipeline runs (viewing inputs and outputs) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

From Monitoring hub, select the latest failed run of Pipeline1, and then view the output JSON: Why it is incorrect: The output JSON is generated after the activity finishes (or fails). It contains the run metrics (number of rows read, time taken, throughput) and the error code or message returned by the source system. Although the SQL server error message might contain a small fragment of the syntax error, it does not record the full dynamic query. The requested query always belongs to the input parameters.

  • Official documentation: Monitor pipeline runs (output details) - Microsoft Learn

From Real-time hub, select Fabric events, and then review the details of Microsoft.Fabric.ItemReadFailed or ItemUpdateFailed: Why they are incorrect: The Real-Time hub and Fabric events are designed for auditing and streaming platform-level or workspace-level events (for example, if a user deleted a report, or if the schema update of an item failed). They are not designed to drill down to the level of internal debugging and capture the dynamic variables of the individual activities that occur inside a data pipeline.

  • Official documentation: Microsoft Fabric workspace events - Microsoft Learn

Monitor pipeline runs (output details) - Microsoft Learn

q066.stem:
You have a Fabric notebook named Notebook1 that has been executing successfully for the last week.

During the last run, Notebook1executed nine jobs.

You need to view the jobs in a timeline chart.

What should you use?
options: the job history from the application run
the run series from the details of the application run

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option E: the run series from the details of the application run.

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Option E: the run series from the details of the application run. Why it is correct: In the notebook monitoring interface in Microsoft Fabric, the Run series feature integrated into the application details provides a visual representation in the form of a trend and timeline chart (timeline chart). This view lets you analyze the behavior and chronological evolution of the jobs run across the runs of the item, exactly meeting the requirement to view the nine jobs on a timeline.

answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Option D: Spark History Server Why it is incorrect: Although the Spark History Server shows timelines of events at the level of low-level engine tasks (Event Timeline), it is designed for deep debugging of Spark code and stages, not for the integrated visualization of the run series that the application details pane in Fabric exposes directly.

  • Official documentation: Monitor Spark applications with the history server - Microsoft Learn

Option A: Real-Time hub Why it is incorrect: The Real-Time Intelligence hub is exclusively responsible for the management, discovery and routing of streaming data flows (such as eventstreams and KQL databases), so it has no link whatsoever to monitoring batch notebooks (batch).

  • Official documentation: Real-Time hub overview in Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Option B: Monitoring hub Why it is incorrect: The Monitoring hub centralizes the overall success or failure status of all the items at the workspace level on a macro level, but it does not include the graphical breakdown of the internal timeline of the jobs of a specific notebook.

  • Official documentation: Use the Monitoring hub in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Option C: the job history from the application run Why it is incorrect: This option describes a traditional tabular list of the jobs run, but it does not offer the structured graphical timeline component (timeline chart) required to meet the question's requirement.

q067.stem:
HOTSPOT -

You have a Fabric workspace that contains an eventstream named EventStream1.

You discover that an EventStream1 transformation fails.

You need to find the following error information:

The error details, including the occurrence time

The total number of errors -

What should you use? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Dropdown 1 (To find the error details): Runtime logs

  • Dropdown 2 (To find the total number of errors): Data insights

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Dropdown 1: Runtime logs Why it is correct: To find the technical details of an error, including the exact failure message and the timestamp (the time of occurrence) of the failed transformation, you must consult the runtime logs. This feature tracks granular operational events at the engine level. It presents a table with the severity level (information, warning, error), the exact time and the diagnostic text, allowing you to debug the problem at a technical level.

  • Official documentation: Monitor eventstreams (view runtime logs) - Microsoft Learn

Dropdown 2: Data insights Why it is correct: To find the total number of errors, you need an aggregated metric (a volume or a sum), not an individual technical record. The Data insights tab provides pre-built visual dashboards and charts that evaluate the performance of the eventstream. It shows cumulative counts over time, such as total input messages, total output messages and the cumulative total of errors or degraded messages.

  • Official documentation: Monitor eventstreams (view data insights) - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Data preview: Why it is incorrect: This feature is used exclusively to view a raw sample of the content of the messages (the actual payload in JSON, CSV, etc. format) flowing through a node at that moment. Its purpose is to help the engineer visually verify that the columns and data types are correct. It does not capture system logs, does not show transformation execution errors and does not keep a cumulative count of failures.

  • Official documentation: Data preview in eventstreams - Microsoft Learn

Details: Why it is incorrect: The Details pane is simply a static administrative view of the item's properties within Microsoft Fabric. It shows the item's metadata, such as who created it, the unique workspace identifier, the creation date and the Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels applied. It is not a telemetry tool, so it will never show transformation errors or operational counts.

  • Official documentation: View item details in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

q068.stem:
You need to ensure that processes for the bronze and silver layers run in isolation.

How should you configure the Apache Spark settings?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: Disable high concurrency.

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Disable high concurrency: Why it is correct: The case study explicitly states that "high concurrency is enabled for Workspace1". In Microsoft Fabric, the Apache Spark high concurrency mode lets multiple notebooks share a single active Spark session. This is excellent for saving startup time and optimizing resources, but it completely eliminates logical isolation, because the processes share the context, memory, variables and temporary views.

The strict business requirement is to ensure that the bronze and silver layer processes are run in isolation. The only way to force each notebook or process to start its own dedicated session, clean and separate from the other runs, is to disable the high concurrency setting.

  • Official documentation: High concurrency mode in Apache Spark for Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Create a custom pool: Why it is incorrect: A custom pool is used to define physical hardware characteristics (such as node size, the virtual machine family or autoscale rules). Configuring a custom pool does not guarantee isolation, because you can have a custom pool with high concurrency turned on, causing the processes to still be mixed in the same session.

  • Official documentation: Configure Spark pools in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Modify the number of executors: Why it is incorrect: (Note: this refers to the technical term "executors" from the original English exam.) Modifying the number of executors simply changes the number of workers and the compute power allocated to a Spark job so that it runs faster. It has no relationship with session isolation between different processes or layers of the medallion architecture.

  • Official documentation: Apache Spark resource management (executors) - Microsoft Learn

Set the default environment: Why it is incorrect: In Fabric, an environment is an item used to package public or custom libraries (Python, R, Java packages) and general engine properties. Although you can associate an environment with a workspace, this does not disable the session-sharing behavior (high concurrency) that causes the lack of isolation problem.

  • Official documentation: Create, configure, and use an environment in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Configure Spark pools in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
Apache Spark resource management (executors) - Microsoft Learn

q069.stem:
You need to ensure that the authors can see only their respective sales data.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, drag the appropriate values the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Box 1 (WITH): SCHEMABINDING

  • Box 2 (WHERE @Author =): USER_NAME()

  • Box 3 (ON): AuthorSales

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Box 1: SCHEMABINDING Why it is correct: To implement row-level security (RLS) in SQL Server and in Microsoft Fabric data warehousing, it is a strict architectural requirement that the inline table-valued function (TVF) be created by using the SCHEMABINDING option. This "locks" the structure of the tables or objects the function references, preventing them from being modified or dropped in a way that would break the security rule.

  • Official documentation: Implement row-level security (RLS) - Microsoft Learn

Box 2: USER_NAME() Why it is correct: The case study explicitly specifies that authors "authenticate to a Fabric guest tenant by using their email address". In the SQL engine, the USER_NAME() system function returns the user name of the current session, which in this Azure Active Directory/Microsoft Entra ID environment corresponds exactly to the email address the author signed in with. By equating the @Author parameter (which will receive the value of the AuthorEmail column) with USER_NAME(), we guarantee that each author sees only the rows where their email matches.

  • Official documentation: The USER_NAME() function in Transact-SQL - Microsoft Learn

Box 3: AuthorSales Why it is correct: The CREATE SECURITY POLICY statement requires you to specify which physical table the security filter will be applied to. The scenario states that "A table named AuthorSales stores the sales data related to each author". Therefore, the policy must be applied ON AuthorSales, using the previously created function as the filter.

  • Official documentation: Implement row-level security (RLS) in Fabric data warehousing - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

BLOCK / FILTER: Why they are incorrect: These two words are types of security predicates in SQL Server. A FILTER predicate silently restricts the rows that are available for read operations, while a BLOCK predicate explicitly blocks the write operations that violate the rule. In the code snippet provided, the CREATE SECURITY POLICY statement already explicitly includes the text ADD FILTER PREDICATE, so neither of these two words is necessary. In addition, they are not valid commands for the function's WITH clause, they do not represent the session user, and they are not tables.

  • Official documentation: CREATE SECURITY POLICY (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

AuthorEmail / AuthorSales.AuthorEmail: Why they are incorrect: These are column names. In Box 2, we need to compare the @Author parameter against the identity of the user running the query (USER_NAME()). If we used AuthorEmail in Box 2, the function would compare the value with itself, which would always return true and completely nullify the security isolation. In Box 3 we need the name of the base table (AuthorSales) that the policy will be applied to, not the name of one of its columns.

INLINE: Why it is incorrect: Implementing row-level security (RLS) requires creating an "inline table-valued function". However, the word INLINE is not a syntactically valid keyword within the Transact-SQL WITH clause when running a CREATE FUNCTION command. The mandatory syntax that seals the structure for RLS is SCHEMABINDING.

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option: Yes

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Why the answer is Yes: The scenario's goal is to securely retrieve credentials (the application ID and the secret) stored in Azure Key Vault in order to generate an authentication token from a Microsoft Fabric notebook, without exposing that confidential data in plain text.

In Microsoft Fabric, the native and recommended library for interacting with Azure Key Vault from a notebook is notebookutils (which is the evolution and direct alias of mssparkutils in Fabric). The specific notebookutils.credentials.getSecret method is designed exactly for this purpose. By passing it the Key Vault URL and the Key Vault secret name as parameters, the notebook connects to the service and securely extracts the value at run time. This solution perfectly and directly meets the technical and security goal.

  • Official documentation: Use notebookutils for credentials and Azure Key Vault in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect option

Why the No option is incorrect: Selecting "No" would mean wrongly believing that Fabric notebooks cannot natively connect to Azure Key Vault, or that it is mandatory to install complex external Python libraries (such as azure-keyvault-secrets from the Azure SDK) to achieve it. Although using the standard Azure SDK is a technically possible alternative, using the built-in notebookutils utility is the official, cleaner and fully supported path within the Spark ecosystem in Fabric.

You have an Azure key vault named KeyVault1 that contains secrets.

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1. Workspace contains a notebook named Notebook1 that performs the following tasks:

• Loads stage data to the target tables in a lakehouse

• Triggers the refresh of a semantic model

You plan to add functionality to Notebook1 that will use the Fabric API to monitor the semantic model refreshes.

You need to retrieve the registered application ID and secret from KeyVault1 to generate the authentication token.

Solution: You use the following code segment:

Use notebookutils.credentials.putSecret and specify the key vault URL and key vault secret.

Does this meet the goal?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option: No

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Why the answer is No: The explicit goal of the scenario is to retrieve (read) the credentials stored in Azure Key Vault so they can be used to generate a token. However, the proposed solution suggests using the notebookutils.credentials.putSecret method.

In the Microsoft Fabric utilities library, the putSecret command is a write operation designed to create, save or update a secret in the environment. It does not return the secret value to the notebook. Trying to use a write command to perform a read task will completely fail to achieve the goal of obtaining the application ID and the password. As we saw in the previous variant of this series, the correct and exclusive command to retrieve information is getSecret.

  • Official documentation: Use notebookutils for credentials (putSecret versus getSecret) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect option

Why the Yes option is incorrect: Selecting "Yes" makes a serious conceptual mistake between data input/output (I/O) operations. It confuses the act of securely storing a value (put) with the act of extracting it for consumption (get). If putSecret is run in this context, the code will not only fail to return the necessary credentials to the notebook variables, but it could also try to overwrite the existing secret if the security context allows it, causing a disruption in the process.

q073.stem:
DRAG DROP

-

You have two Fabric notebooks named Load_Salesperson and Load_Orders that read data from Parquet files in a lakehouse. Load_Salesperson writes to a Delta table named dim_salesperson. Load_Orders writes to a Delta table named fact_orders and is dependent on the successful execution of Load_Salesperson.

You need to implement a pattern to dynamically execute Load_Salesperson and Load_Orders in the appropriate order by using a notebook.

How should you complete the code? To answer, drag the appropriate values the correct targets. Each value may be used once, more than once, or not at all. You may need to drag the split bar between panes or scroll to view content.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

Box 1 (JSON array root): activities
Box 2 (Execution relationship): dependencies
Box 3 (Execution method): runMultiple

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Box 1: activities Why it is correct: In the Microsoft Spark utilities (mssparkutils) API, to define a directed acyclic graph (DAG) by using JSON, the official schema strictly requires the root node to be named activities. This parameter defines an array that works as the main container, inside which all the dictionaries with the individual configuration of each notebook that will take part in the flow are declared.

  • Official documentation: DAG structure and the 'activities' array in Spark utilities - Microsoft Learn

Box 2: dependencies Why it is correct: Inside the activities array, each notebook can run in parallel or sequentially. To force an order (as the scenario requires, where Load_Orders depends on Load_Salesperson), the JSON schema uses the dependencies property. By including this property and passing the name of the previous activity as its value, the engine blocks the execution of the second notebook until the first one has returned a success status.

  • Official documentation: Defining dependencies ('dependencies') in multiple runs - Microsoft Learn

Box 3: runMultiple Why it is correct: The notebook module of the mssparkutils library exposes different methods depending on the complexity of the task. While the standard run method is used to launch a single notebook, the runMultiple method is designed exclusively to take the complete JSON object (the DAG) that we just built, interpret the activities and dependencies properties, and orchestrate the whole workload on the cluster**.**

  • Official documentation: The mssparkutils.notebook runMultiple method - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

notebooks: Why it is incorrect: Although it might intuitively seem like the logical name for the main array of the JSON, the Microsoft Fabric parsing engine requires a strict schema. The documentation defines that the base dictionary of the directed acyclic graph (DAG) must contain the root key activities. If you use the word notebooks instead, the method will not recognize the list of tasks and execution will fail immediately with a schema validation error.

  • Official documentation: JSON syntax for runMultiple in Spark utilities - Microsoft Learn

execute: Why it is incorrect: In the Microsoft Spark utilities (mssparkutils) ecosystem, the module dedicated to notebook management (notebook) exposes very specific control commands. To start the execution of other code, the official API supports only the run method (for sequential execution of a single notebook) and the runMultiple method (for complex DAG-based executions). The execute method does not exist in this library; trying to call it will cause a Python attribute error (AttributeError).

  • Official documentation: Notebook utilities API reference - Microsoft Learn

broadcast: Why it is incorrect: The word broadcast is an advanced optimization concept of the Apache Spark core. It is used to send copies of small tables (dimensions) or variables directly to the memory of all worker nodes to avoid transferring data over the network during join operations (broadcast hash join). It is an internal data transformation command, so it has no relationship with orchestration, scheduling or dependency management between notebooks.

  • Official documentation: Optimizing joins with broadcast in Apache Spark - Microsoft Learn

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains a warehouse named Warehouse2.

A team of data analysts has Viewer role access to Workspace1.

You create a table by running the following statement.

You need to ensure that the team can view only the first two characters and the last four characters of the CreditCard attribute.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Drop-down 1 (Action on the table): ALTER

  • Drop-down 2 (Action on the column): ALTER

  • Drop-down 3 (Masking function): PARTIAL

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Drop-down 1: ALTER Why it is correct: In the scenario, the dbo.CreditCard table has already been created in the data warehouse (as the first block of code provided shows). To modify the structure or the security policies of an object that already exists in Transact-SQL, the main data definition command to use is ALTER. In this case, the complete statement must begin with ALTER TABLE.

  • Official documentation: ALTER TABLE statement (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 2: ALTER Why it is correct: Once the table to modify has been specified, you must indicate at which component level the change will be applied. To apply a dynamic data masking policy to a specific attribute, strict SQL syntax requires the ALTER COLUMN command, followed by the column name and the ADD MASKED statement.

  • Official documentation: Syntax for altering columns and adding masking - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 3: PARTIAL Why it is correct: The business requirement states that analysts must see only the first two characters and the last four. In the data masking engine, the PARTIAL function is designed exactly to build this logic. It takes three parameters: the number of leading characters to show (2), the literal padding string ("XXXXXXXXXX") and the number of trailing characters to show (4).

  • Official documentation: Dynamic data masking - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

CREATE: Why it is incorrect: The CREATE command is used to instantiate new objects from scratch. Since the table already physically exists in the database, trying to use CREATE TABLE in this context would generate an error saying that the object already exists. To modify an existing schema, the mandatory statement is ALTER.

  • Official documentation: CREATE TABLE (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

DEFAULT: Why it is incorrect: As a masking function, DEFAULT hides the entire contents of the cell (replacing text with "XXXX", for example). This directly violates the business requirement to show the first two and last four characters of the real value.

  • Official documentation: Dynamic data masking (DEFAULT function) - Microsoft Learn

DROP: Why it is incorrect: DROP is a destructive data definition (DDL) command. If you use DROP TABLE or ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN, you will physically delete the table or the column from the model. Running this would destroy the credit card information instead of masking it.

  • Official documentation: ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

EMAIL: Why it is incorrect: The EMAIL masking function is preconfigured exclusively to detect and hide email addresses. It exposes the first letter and hides the rest up to the domain (for example, aXXX@XXXX.com). It does not support inserting custom numeric parameters (2, 4) as this exercise requires.

  • Official documentation: Dynamic data masking (EMAIL function) - Microsoft Learn

REPLACE: Why it is incorrect: REPLACE is a scalar string function used in SELECT or UPDATE queries to substitute characters. It is not a valid security command, and there is no dynamic data masking directive (ADD MASKED) called REPLACE in Transact-SQL.

  • Official documentation: REPLACE (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

UPDATE: Why it is incorrect: UPDATE is a data manipulation (DML) command that permanently alters the physical records stored on disk. Dynamic masking aims to hide the data only at query time (on the fly) based on the user's permissions, keeping the real data intact in the underlying tables.

  • Official documentation: UPDATE (Transact-SQL) - Microsoft Learn

You are building a data orchestration pattern by using a Fabric data pipeline named Dynamic Data Copy as shown in the exhibit. (Click the Exhibit tab.)

Dynamic Data Copy does NOT use parametrization.

You need to configure the ForEach activity to receive the list of tables to be copied.

How should you complete the pipeline expression? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Drop-down 1: Lookup Schema and Table

  • Drop-down 2: output.value

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Drop-down 1: Lookup Schema and Table Why it is correct: In Microsoft Fabric and Azure Data Factory orchestration, the ForEach activity needs to receive an array of items to iterate over. This array comes from the output of the immediately preceding activity. Looking at the pipeline canvas, we can clearly see that the previous activity connected by the success arrow (the green line) to the ForEach block is named exactly "Lookup Schema and Table". Therefore, the dynamic expression must reference the name of this specific activity inside the @activity('...') function.

  • Official documentation: Lookup activity in data pipelines - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 2: output.value Why it is correct: The Lookup activity, when configured to return multiple rows (for example, a list of tables), wraps its results inside a JSON array. In pipeline expression syntax, the attribute that holds the full list of those returned rows is always called value, which is contained within the output. Therefore, by concatenating @activity('Lookup Schema and Table').output.value, you correctly hand the complete set of records to the ForEach iterator.

  • Official documentation: ForEach activity in data pipelines - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Incorrect options for Drop-down 1:

Batch Object Copy: Why it is incorrect: If you look at the canvas, "Batch Object Copy" is the copy activity that lives inside the ForEach loop (in the lower box). It cannot be the data source that feeds the very loop that contains it. Trying to reference an inner activity from the container's configuration will cause a circular dependency error in the expression.

  • Official documentation: Expressions and functions in Azure Data Factory and Fabric - Microsoft Learn

Dynamic Data Copy: Why it is incorrect: According to the scenario description, "Dynamic Data Copy" is the global name of the entire pipeline, not the name of the source (Lookup) activity that generates the data. The @activity() function strictly requires the name of a valid inner activity block, not the name of the parent pipeline.

  • Official documentation: Activity function reference - Microsoft Learn

Extraction Loop: Why it is incorrect: "Extraction Loop" is the name of the ForEach activity itself. Trying to reference the activity itself in its own "Items" property (the items to iterate over) would cause a self-reference error at schema validation time, since it cannot read its own data before it runs.

  • Official documentation: Activity control flow in pipelines - Microsoft Learn

Incorrect options for Drop-down 2:

output: Why it is incorrect: Calling only .output will return the complete JSON object of the Lookup activity. This main object contains not only the data (the value) but also execution metadata such as the row count (count) and timings. The ForEach activity will fail if it receives this composite object instead of directly receiving the array found in the value property.

  • Official documentation: Lookup activity output structure - Microsoft Learn

output.count: Why it is incorrect: The .count property returns a single integer that represents the total number of rows found by the Lookup activity. The ForEach activity requires an array (an iterable set) in its "Items" property, not a simple number. If you pass an integer, execution will fail immediately.

  • Official documentation: Lookup output properties (Count) - <<Microsoft Learn

output.pipelineReturnValue: Why it is incorrect: This property does not belong to the standard output of a Lookup activity. It is used specifically to capture the final return value of a flow when a child pipeline is called by using the Execute Pipeline activity. Referencing it after a Lookup will return a null value and cause an error.

  • Official documentation: Set and use pipeline return values - Microsoft Learn

You have a Fabric workspace that contains a warehouse named Warehouse1.

Warehouse1 contains a table named DimCustomers. DimCustomers contains the following columns:

• CustomerName

• CustomerID

• BirthDate

• EmailAddress

You need to configure security to meet the following requirements:

• BirthDate in DimCustomer must be masked and display 1900-01-01.

• EmailAddress in DimCustomer must be masked and display only the first leading character and the last five characters.

How should you complete the statement? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Drop-down 1: 'default()'

  • Drop-down 2: 'partial(1, "@", 5)'

Detailed analysis of the correct sequence

Drop-down 1: 'default()' Why it is correct: In Transact-SQL dynamic data masking, the default() function automatically adapts to the underlying data type of the column. When applied to date and time data types (such as Date or DateTime), the engine's default behavior is to mask the real value by always returning 1900-01-01 (00:00:00.0000000). This exactly meets the first requirement of the scenario natively, without requiring additional parameters.

  • Official documentation: Dynamic data masking (default function on dates) - Microsoft Learn

Drop-down 2: 'partial(1, "@", 5)' Why it is correct: The requirement strictly states that "only the first leading character and the last five characters" of the email address must be shown. The partial() function is designed to offer this granular level of control over text strings. It requires three exact parameters: the number of characters to reveal at the beginning (1), the literal padding string for the middle part ("@"), and the number of real characters to reveal at the end (5). This formulation maps precisely to the business need.

  • Official documentation: Dynamic data masking (partial function) - Microsoft Learn

Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Incorrect options for Drop-down 1:

'partial(1900-01-01)': Why it is incorrect: The partial function is restricted exclusively to character string data types (varchar, nvarchar, etc.); it does not operate on date data types. In addition, its syntax is strict and requires three parameters (prefix, padding, suffix). Entering a date as the only parameter will cause an immediate syntax validation error when you try to alter the table.

  • Official documentation: Partial masking function rules - Microsoft Learn

'random(1900-01-01, 1900-01-01)': Why it is incorrect: The random masking function is designed only for columns with numeric data types (such as int, bigint, float). Its purpose is to return a random number within a given range. It does not support text strings or date formats, so applying it to the BirthDate column will result in a data type incompatibility error from the SQL engine.

  • Official documentation: Dynamic data masking (random function) - Microsoft Learn

Incorrect options for Drop-down 2:

'default()': Why it is incorrect: If the default function is applied to a text string column such as the email address, the engine's behavior is to hide the entire content and replace it with the value "XXXX". This flatly fails the scenario requirement, since the analysts would lose the ability to see the first character and the last five.

  • Official documentation: Dynamic data masking (default function on strings) - Microsoft Learn

'email()': Why it is incorrect: This is the option designed specifically to confuse in the exam. Although the email() function exists, its pattern is predefined and unchangeable: it shows the first letter of the original email, adds a static "XXX@XXXX" padding, and always ends by returning the ".com" suffix statically, ignoring the user's real domain. It does not let you configure the display of "the last five characters", so it does not meet the specific guidelines of your security team.

  • Official documentation: Dynamic data masking (email function) - Microsoft Learn

'random(1, "@", 5)': Why it is incorrect: As established earlier, the random function requires two integer numeric parameters to define the lower and upper bounds of the random value to generate. Trying to pass text characters or symbols (such as the at sign) instead of integers will cause an immediate compilation failure in the Transact-SQL statement.

  • Official documentation: Required syntax for the random function - Microsoft Learn

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1 that contains the following items:

• A Microsoft Power BI report named Report1

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option E: Lakehouse1, Model1, and Report1 only

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Lakehouse1, Model1, and Report1 only: Why it is correct: In this certification question, the term "recommend" is the literal translation of the governance concept endorsement (which covers the "Promoted" and "Certified" labels) in Microsoft Fabric and Power BI. This feature lets organizations mark high-quality, trusted content so that users can find validated data more easily.

The Microsoft governance framework restricts exactly which items can receive these endorsement labels. The official list of supported items includes Power BI reports (Report1), semantic models (Model1) and lakehouses (Lakehouse1). Therefore, this combination is the only one that names exclusively items that support this governance feature.

  • Official documentation: Endorsement in Microsoft Fabric - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Options A, B, C and D: Why they are incorrect: All of these options are incorrect for one fundamental reason: they include the dashboard (Dashboard1). In the Microsoft Fabric and Power BI governance architecture, dashboards do not support the endorsement feature.

While semantic models, dataflows, reports and apps can be promoted or certified to guide users toward sources of truth, dashboards are considered single-canvas consumption visualization tools that do not fall within this data certification lifecycle. Therefore, any option that suggests applying this governance process to a dashboard is technically not feasible on the platform.

  • Official documentation: Endorse content in Power BI: promotion and certification (supported items) - Microsoft Learn

q078.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1.

Your company acquires GitHub licenses.

You need to configure source control for Workpace1 to use GitHub. The solution must follow the principle of least privilege.

Which permissions do you require to ensure that you can commit code to GitHub?
options: Actions (Read and write) and Contents (Read and write)
Contents (Read) and Commit statuses (Read and write)

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option C: Contents (Read and write) only

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Contents (Read and write) only: Why it is correct: To configure the Microsoft Fabric version control integration with GitHub, the security best practice is to use a fine-grained personal access token (PAT). The scenario strictly requires applying the principle of least privilege (granting only the permissions needed for the task). For the Fabric workspace to be able to read the branch structure and send changes (commit) of the items to the repository, the only API scope you need to enable in GitHub is Contents, set to the Read and write access level. With this single permission, the goal is met securely.

  • Official documentation: Git integration process (permissions for GitHub repositories) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Actions (Read and write) and Contents (Read and write): Why it is incorrect: Although this configuration would allow Fabric to make commits successfully (since it includes the Contents permission), it directly violates the principle of least privilege requirement. The "Actions" permission in GitHub is used exclusively to create, modify, run or stop automated CI/CD workflows. The native Fabric integration does not require any access to the GitHub Actions engine to simply sync and save code.

  • Official documentation: Get started with Git integration - Microsoft Learn

Actions (Read and write) only: Why it is incorrect: This option would cause a total integration failure and block the workflow. The Actions scope does not grant any access to the source code or to the repository files. By omitting the Contents permission, Microsoft Fabric will receive an access denied error (HTTP 403 Forbidden) at the exact moment it tries to connect, read the folder structure or send a commit.

  • Official documentation: Troubleshoot Git integration permissions - Microsoft Learn

Contents (Read) and Commit statuses (Read and write): Why it is incorrect: Assigning Contents only in "Read" mode (read-only) lets Fabric sync or download the code from GitHub into the workspace, but completely prohibits it from sending new changes to the repository (committing). In addition, the "Commit statuses" permission is for external tools to mark a success or failure validation on a code commit, which does not meet the functional goal of saving the work.

  • Official documentation: Git integration limitations and commit rules for Fabric - Microsoft Learn

You have a Fabric workspace named Workspace1.

You plan to configure Git integration for Workspace1 by using an Azure DevOps Git repository.

An Azure DevOps admin creates the required artifacts to support the integration of Workspace1.

Which details do you require to perform the integration?
options: the organization, project, Git repository, and branch
the personal access token (PAT) for Git authentication and the Git repository URL
the project, Git repository, branch, and Git folder
the Git repository URL and the Git folder

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: the organization, project, Git repository, and branch

Detailed analysis of the correct option

the organization, project, Git repository, and branch: Why it is correct: In Microsoft Fabric, native integration with Azure DevOps is highly optimized thanks to the shared Microsoft ecosystem. Fabric uses your current user identity (Microsoft Entra ID) to authenticate automatically (single sign-on) against Azure DevOps. Because of this native connection, the Git settings pane in Fabric does not ask you for complex URLs or manual tokens. Instead, it displays a series of drop-down menus where you must hierarchically select exactly these four items: the organization, the project within that organization, the specific Git repository, and finally the branch that will be synced with the workspace.

  • Official documentation: Get started with Git integration (connect to Azure DevOps) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

the personal access token (PAT) for Git authentication and the Git repository URL: Why it is incorrect: This combination of data is exactly what is required when you connect the Fabric workspace to GitHub, not to Azure DevOps. As we saw in the previous question in the series, GitHub requires a personal access token (PAT) and the direct repository URL to authorize the connection. For Azure DevOps, Fabric takes advantage of seamless native authentication, so it will never ask you for a PAT or to paste the URL.

  • Official documentation: Get started with Git integration (connect to GitHub) - Microsoft Learn

the project, Git repository, branch, and Git folder: Why it is incorrect: This option is missing a critical parameter of the hierarchy: the organization. In the Azure DevOps architecture, projects do not float in a vacuum; they necessarily reside within organizations. If you do not select the organization, Fabric cannot locate the project. In addition, the Git folder parameter is a completely optional setting used to restrict syncing to a specific directory; it is not a mandatory requirement for establishing the initial connection.

  • Official documentation: Git integration process and hierarchy in Fabric - Microsoft Learn

the Git repository URL and the Git folder: Why it is incorrect: As in the previous cases, the native setup flow for Azure DevOps in Fabric does not work by pasting a flat repository URL. The system is designed so that you navigate through built-in drop-down menus. Moreover, trying to configure a connection by providing only a URL and an optional folder would completely ignore the branch, leaving the system without knowing which code commit point the workspace should connect to.

  • Official documentation: Troubleshoot Git connection issues and requirements - Microsoft Learn

q080.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a lakehouse and a semantic model named Model1.

You use a notebook named Notebook1 to ingest and transform data from an external data source.

You need to execute Notebook1 as part of a data pipeline named Pipeline1. The process must meet the following requirements:

• Run daily at 07:00 AM UTC.

• Attempt to retry Notebook1 twice if the notebook fails.

• After Notebook1 executes successfully, refresh Model1.

Which three actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.

NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.
options: Place the Semantic model refresh activity after the Notebook activity and link the activities by using the On success condition.
From the Schedule settings of Pipeline1, set the time zone to UTC.
Set the Retry setting of the Notebook activity to 2.
From the Schedule settings of Notebook1, set the time zone to UTC.
Set the Retry setting of the Semantic model refresh activity to 2.
Place the Semantic model refresh activity after the Notebook activity and link the activities by using an On completion condition.

answer.correct:
Correct answers:

  • Option A: Place the Semantic model refresh activity after the Notebook activity and link the activities by using the On success condition.

  • Option B: From the Schedule settings of Pipeline1, set the time zone to UTC.

  • Option C: Set the Retry setting of the Notebook activity to 2.

Detailed analysis of the correct options

Option A: Place the Semantic model refresh activity after the Notebook activity and link the activities by using the On success condition. Why it is correct: The business requirement specifies that the semantic model must be refreshed "After Notebook1 runs successfully". In Fabric pipelines, dependencies between activities are defined by colored links. The green "On success" link ensures that the flow moves to the refresh activity if, and only if, the notebook code finished without returning any error.

  • Official documentation: Pipeline control flow (success dependencies) - Microsoft Learn

Option B: From the Schedule settings of Pipeline1, set the time zone to UTC. Why it is correct: The scenario requires running this process "as part of a data pipeline named Pipeline1". To achieve this, the scheduled trigger must be configured at the parent pipeline level, not on the individual items. By setting the Pipeline1 schedule to 07:00 AM and explicitly selecting the UTC time zone, you guarantee that the entire orchestration (the notebook followed by the refresh) starts at the exact time the business requires.

  • Official documentation: Schedule data pipeline runs - Microsoft Learn

Option C: Set the Retry setting of the Notebook activity to 2. Why it is correct: The mandate is explicit: "Retry Notebook1 twice if it fails". On the "General" tab of the Notebook activity settings on the pipeline canvas, there is a property called "Retry". Setting this value to 2 configures the engine to automatically restart that specific activity up to two additional times in case of failure, without affecting the rest of the flow.

  • Official documentation: General activity settings (Retry property) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Option D: From the Schedule settings of Notebook1, set the time zone to UTC. Why it is incorrect: Although it is possible to schedule a notebook directly from its own interface, the scenario sets a strict requirement: "You need to run Notebook1 as part of a data pipeline named Pipeline1". If you schedule the notebook on its own, its execution will be orphaned and disconnected from the pipeline, breaking the orchestration sequence that must subsequently trigger the semantic model refresh.

  • Official documentation: Differences between scheduling notebooks and scheduling pipelines - Microsoft Learn

Option E: Set the Retry setting of the Semantic model refresh activity to 2. Why it is incorrect: This option applies the fault-tolerance logic to the wrong component. The business requirement specifically asks for Notebook1 to be retried if it fails, probably because external sources may suffer temporary network outages. Placing the retries on the semantic model will not solve a possible failure in the notebook's data ingestion.

  • Official documentation: Fault tolerance in Fabric data pipelines - Microsoft Learn

Option F: Place the Semantic model refresh activity after the Notebook activity and link the activities by using an On completion condition. Why it is incorrect: The "On completion" link (represented by a blue arrow) is an unconditional dependency. It tells the engine to trigger the next activity regardless of whether the previous activity succeeded or failed with a fatal error. This flatly violates the rule requiring the model to be refreshed only after a "successful" run. If the notebook fails and this option is used, the semantic model will try to refresh by consuming empty or corrupt data.

  • Official documentation: Routing conditions in pipelines (On completion) - Microsoft Learn

q081.stem:
You have a Fabric workspace that contains a lakehouse named Lakehouse1.

You plan to create a data pipeline named Pipeline1 to ingest data into Lakehouse1. You will use a parameter named param1 to pass an external value into Pipeline1. The param1 parameter has a data type of int.

You need to ensure that the pipeline expression returns param1 as an int value.

How should you specify the parameter value?

answer.correct:
Correct answer:

  • Option A: "@pipeline().parameters.param1"

Detailed analysis of the correct option

Option A: "@pipeline().parameters.param1" Why it is correct: In the expression language of data pipelines in Microsoft Fabric (based on Azure Data Factory), the way you wrap the expression determines the resulting data type. By placing a single at sign immediately followed by the expression without using curly braces, you are telling the evaluation engine to extract the value and strictly preserve its original data type. Since the scenario specifies that param1 is of type int, this exact syntax will return the value as a pure integer, meeting the goal 100%.

  • Official documentation: Expressions in data pipelines (evaluation and data type preservation) - Microsoft Learn
answer.incorrect:
Detailed analysis of the incorrect options

Option B: "@{pipeline().parameters.param1}" Why it is incorrect: Using curly braces around the expression invokes the feature known as string interpolation. Although the engine will correctly read the numeric value stored in param1, interpolation will mechanically force an implicit conversion of that result to a text (string) data type. Since the business requirement demands returning an int, this option would pass a text value (for example, "50" instead of the number 50) and could cause errors in the target activity.

  • Official documentation: String interpolation in data pipelines - Microsoft Learn

Option C: "@{pipeline().parameters. [param1]}" Why it is incorrect: This option has two critical flaws. The first is that it uses string interpolation braces, which would destroy the int data type by converting it to text, just like the previous option. The second flaw is purely syntactic: inserting a blank space and using bracket notation after the dot operator is illegal syntax in this engine. This would cause a compilation error (parse error) and the pipeline would fail before running.

  • Official documentation: Expression language syntax details - Microsoft Learn

Option D: "@@{pipeline().parameters.param1}" Why it is incorrect: In this expression engine, placing two consecutive at signs at the start of a statement acts as an escape character. Its function is to cancel the evaluation of variables. If you use this option, the engine will not look up the value of param1. Instead, it will return a literal static text equivalent to the string @{pipeline().parameters.param1}. This completely fails the goal of retrieving the parameter.

  • Official documentation: Use escape characters in pipeline expressions - Microsoft Learn
